A conditional clause attached to a statement about the future. It has been the ordinary Arabic qualifier for anything not yet done ever since, used in speech far outside religious settings.
A form of the verb meaning to find the way, with an emphatic particle attached. The confidence in the word sits oddly beside the condition preceding it, and the pairing is the sentence's whole shape.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Anyone who kept cattle in an oasis would recognise the complaint. Cows of the same stock look alike at a distance, and herds mixed at the watering places and had to be separated again, which is why owners cut marks into ears or dyed patches of hide. Telling one animal from another was a practical daily skill, and saying they all look the same was, in that setting, an admission as much as an excuse.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase these questioners add is the one the Quran elsewhere instructs a person never to leave off, telling the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) not to say of anything that he will do it tomorrow without adding it. That instruction comes with a reported occasion of its own, and the phrase has been ordinary Arabic speech ever since.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Referring an outcome to God's will is presented here as the thing that unblocks a stalled search, and its placement matters. It arrives at the end of a third repeated question, after the requirement has already become expensive, so it is not the confident opening of a person who expects things to go well. The passage suggests that the qualification is available late and still works, which is a modest but genuine consolation.

crossReferences.why: Instructs directly that nothing be said about tomorrow without attaching this same qualification.
Has Abraham's son use the phrase at the hardest possible moment, saying he will be found steadfast.
Uses the same root for resemblance earlier in this surah, of fruit given in the Garden.

studies.applyIt: Attach the qualification to one plan today, out loud, and mean it rather than saying it as a habit. Not a large plan. Something you fully expect to happen this afternoon. Notice what it changes about how tightly you are holding the outcome, which is the whole content of the phrase.

studies.title: Now You Have Brought The Truth
studies.meaning: The last specification rules out an animal that has ever worked, and adds that it must carry no mark at all. Since a cow's value in that world lay in ploughing and drawing water, this describes something rare and expensive. Their reply concedes the point, and the narrative then adds a short clause that reads like an aside: they nearly did not do it. The next ayah supplies what the whole sequence was for, a killing and a dispute over who was responsible.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the questioning and turning to the reason behind the instruction. The Quran withholds the occasion until this point, so a reader meets the demand, the resistance and the escalating cost before learning what any of it was about. Commentators note the ordering and read the concealed motive as the key to the episode, since a slaughtered animal was about to expose something a community was covering.

keyTerms.note: Used of an animal trained to the yoke. Its root also gives the word for lowness used earlier in this surah, so the same letters describe a beast made docile and a condition of reduced standing.
From the root that gives the words for peace, safety and submission. Applied to an animal it means delivered whole and unimpaired, with nothing missing and nothing wrong.

A spot of contrasting colour in a coat. Herders used exactly such markings to tell their animals apart, so requiring the absence of one made the beast both unusual and difficult to identify by ownership.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An unsolved killing was the most dangerous situation an Arabian community faced. A body found with no known killer put suspicion on everyone and could open a feud between clans that outlasted the people involved, since blood claims were inherited. Procedures existed for allocating responsibility by sworn oath when evidence ran out, precisely because the alternative was a war nobody had chosen.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the animal as broken to work shares its three root letters with the word for humiliation used ten ayat earlier in this same surah. Both describe being brought low and made tractable, one of a beast under a yoke and one of a people's condition, and the pairing is visible only in the Arabic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The narrative is arranged so that the cost of delay is felt before the purpose is revealed. What began as a plain instruction became an expensive one entirely through the questioning, and the aside about nearly not doing it records how close the whole thing came to failing. The following ayah then names the real subject, and it is concealment. A community was holding something back, and the elaborate procedure existed to bring it out.

crossReferences.why: Tells of another killing and a body concealed, with a bird sent to show how to bury it.
States earlier in this surah that God knows what is disclosed and what is being held back.
Describes people hiding from others what cannot be hidden from God, who is with them as they plan.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you delayed by asking for more information, and price the delay honestly: what it cost in money, time, or in the thing itself getting harder. Do it for one case, in writing. This passage lets the reader feel that cost before explaining anything, which is a good order for reviewing your own.

studies.title: Struck With Part Of It
studies.meaning: The instruction is brief and the outcome is left unstated: strike him with part of it. What the ayah reports instead is the meaning of what happened, and it gives two. A killing is resolved, and a demonstration is provided of how God gives life to the dead. The instrument is worth noticing. Life is restored by means of a slaughtered animal, so the sign is built out of the very thing that had been so expensive to obtain. The closing clause names reason as the faculty being addressed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, concluding the episode that gives this surah its name. The Quran does not narrate the moment of revival or report what was said, moving straight to the general statement. Classical commentators pass on various details of what followed, and are aware that the text itself supplies none of them, so they distinguish what the ayah says from what the reports add.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for striking, addressed to the community rather than to an individual. The same verb is used across the Quran for setting forth a parable, which is a separate and much discussed usage.
A form meaning to cause to live, from the root behind the word for life itself. The Quran uses it of reviving dead earth after rain as often as of raising human beings.
One word covers a natural sign, a miracle and a verse of the Quran. A reader meets it here as a token shown, having already been reading the same word as a name for the text itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An unidentified killer was the one problem Arabian custom handled worst. Compensation could settle an acknowledged killing, and oaths could apportion responsibility when a body was found among a known group, but a genuine unknown left every family exposed to suspicion. Communities lived for years with such cases unresolved. Something that named the responsible party outright ended the specific danger of the whole situation.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran's word for a sign is the same word it uses for one of its own verses, so a person reading this ayah encounters the term twice over: as the token being described and as the unit of text they are reading it in. The double use is present throughout the Quran and never distinguished by a different word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: One event is made to serve two purposes at once, settling a particular dispute and standing as evidence for a general claim. That is how the Quran usually presents signs, as ordinary occurrences carrying more than their occasion. The closing clause is the notable part. Having described something entirely outside experience, the passage asks for reason rather than for awe, which assumes that the argument from a single revival to a general resurrection is one a person can actually follow.

crossReferences.why: Shows Abraham asking to see how the dead are given life, and being shown with birds.
Points to earth revived after its death as the pattern for how the dead will be raised.
States the conclusion directly, that God is the Truth and gives life to the dead.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing today that has come back after appearing finished: a plant after cutting, a friendship after silence, energy after illness. Notice that you accept this without difficulty when it happens on a small scale. The argument in this ayah is asking you to follow that acceptance one step further, using reason rather than feeling.

studies.title: Harder Than The Stones
studies.meaning: The comparison is graded rather than absolute. Hearts became like stone, the ayah says, or harder, and it then proves the qualification by listing three things stone does. Rivers burst from some. Others split and water comes out. Others come down out of awe. Commentators differ over the third item, some reading it plainly and others as a way of speaking, but the structure works either way. Three degrees of yielding are named, and the heart in question is placed beneath all of them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the account of a dead man restored in front of witnesses. The placement is the argument. Classical commentators read the hardening as following directly on a sign of the most unanswerable kind, and note that the surah has by this point recorded several such sequences, in which something extraordinary is seen and the response to it fades within a few lines of text.

keyTerms.note: The verb used of stone and of ground baked hard. Applied to a heart it describes a physical change of texture rather than a decision, which is why the ayah answers it with more physical description.
An intensive form of the verb for cleaving, suggesting splitting along a seam rather than shattering. The word allows for a rock that yields under pressure without ceasing to be a rock.
Lexicographers distinguish this from ordinary fright: it is a fear grounded in knowing what is before you. The Quran attaches it to those who know, which is why it can be ascribed to stone here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: All three of these are things people in Arabia actually saw stone do. Springs emerged from rock faces and fed the wells that settlements were built around. Cliffs seeped after rain, and water was collected from the seams. And rockfall down a wadi side, sudden and heavy, was a known hazard of travelling through gorges in the wet season. The list is observation, not invention.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah does not simply call the hearts stony. It says like stones, or harder, and then spends the rest of its length arguing that even the comparison was generous. Three separate ways in which rock yields are set out one after another, so the passage concedes its own image and then withdraws it as insufficient.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardness is described here as a condition rather than a verdict, which matters for what can be done about it. Something hard has a texture, and texture can change, which is why the Quran speaks elsewhere of hearts being opened and softened. The passage also locates responsiveness in unlikely places. If stone can yield in three distinct ways, then the absence of yielding in a person is not explained by the material they are made of.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether the time has not come for hearts to soften, warning against the hardening that followed earlier scripture.
Contrasts a breast opened to submission with hearts hardened against the remembrance of God.
Says a mountain would have split from awe had this Quran been sent down upon it.

studies.applyIt: Notice something today that used to move you and does not any more: a passage, a piece of news, a person's difficulty. Do not manufacture a feeling about it. Just register the change accurately, and note roughly when it happened. Hardening is gradual and almost always goes unnoticed at the time.

studies.title: After They Had Understood It
studies.meaning: The address turns to the believers and lowers an expectation. Notice how carefully the sentence is limited: a group of them, not all, and used to, in the past. The verb for what that group did comes from the word for the edge of a thing, so the picture is of turning something so it is no longer seen straight on. Commentators divide on whether this describes altering wording or altering the sense given to it, and both readings are standard. The final clause is the weight of the sentence: they had understood it first.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section addressed to those who possessed earlier scripture, and spoken here about them rather than to them. Classical commentators are careful with the limitations built into the wording and generally repeat them, noting that the Quran elsewhere in this same surah describes a portion of the same community standing through the night in recitation. The passage is about a practice, not a people.

keyTerms.note: A portion separated off from a larger body, from the root meaning to divide. The word itself does the limiting, and commentators lean on it when explaining the scope of what follows.
From the noun for the edge of something, and also for a letter of the alphabet. To do this to a text is to turn it onto its edge so that it is no longer being looked at squarely.
The root means to tie or tether, as a camel is hobbled to stop it wandering. Understanding in Arabic is what fastens a thing down, which is why the word also gives the ordinary term for the mind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Where almost nobody could read, whoever could read held a position. A scholar's account of what a passage said settled questions that no listener was able to check, and this was true in every scripture community of the region. The gap between a text and the explanation of it was invisible to the audience by definition. That is not an accusation against anyone in particular. It is a description of how authority worked.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for understanding comes from the verb for tethering an animal so it cannot stray. The ordinary Arabic word for the mind is built from the same root. Reason, in the language of the Quran, is named after the act of tying something down so that it stays where you left it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause about having understood first is what makes this a serious charge rather than an ordinary one. Misreading is a mistake; shifting something you have grasped is a decision, and the passage adds knowingly at the end to close off any remaining ambiguity. It also sets a warning that applies well beyond its occasion, since understanding a text is exactly the condition required before anyone is able to bend it.

crossReferences.why: Describes words being displaced from their positions and speech twisted with the tongue while listening.
Connects hardened hearts with words moved from their proper places after a covenant was set aside.
Speaks of a revelation made into sheets, some of it shown and much of it kept out of sight.

studies.applyIt: Take something you know well, a text or a rule or an agreement, and ask whether you have a habitual reading of one part that is convenient for you. Everyone has at least one. Say the plain sense of it out loud once, without your usual gloss attached, and see whether the two versions differ.

studies.title: What Was Opened To You
studies.meaning: A scene in two halves, and the second half contains a reason that gives everything away. The concern voiced in private is that shared knowledge will be used in argument against them before their Lord. Commentators point out what that concedes: nobody worries about being argued with using something false. The verb for what God has disclosed is the one used for opening a door and for granting a victory, so what they are proposing to withhold is described as something given to them rather than acquired.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's account of encounters between the young community and its neighbours in the city. Classical commentators describe a general pattern of exchanges rather than reporting one occasion, and note that the passage records private speech, which by its nature is reported rather than witnessed. The closing question is addressed to those speaking, not to the believers who are the subject of the first clause.

keyTerms.note: The verb for opening a door and, across the Quran, for granting a decisive victory. Applied to knowledge it presents what they hold as something unlocked for them rather than earned.

keyTerms.gloss: so they may argue against you
keyTerms.note: From the word for a proof or an argument that stands. The form implies a contest between two parties, so the fear is not of being contradicted but of being out-argued with their own material.
The verb for a space emptied of everyone else. The surah used it much earlier of another group withdrawing into private company, so the same word marks both scenes of a second conversation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Knowledge was capital in a society that wrote almost nothing down. A route through country without landmarks, the location of a seasonal well, a genealogy that settled a claim, the wording of an old agreement: each of these was worth something precisely because few people had it. Keeping such things inside a family was ordinary prudence, not meanness. The instinct being described here was the normal management of a scarce asset.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah repeats a construction the surah used some sixty ayat earlier about a different group, down to the same verb for withdrawing into private company and the same reported sentence when meeting believers. The echo is close enough that a reader working through the surah in order meets the earlier scene again in a new setting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reasoning quoted here contains its own refutation, which is why the passage lets it stand without comment and then asks whether they use reason. Someone who fears that a piece of knowledge will count against him before God has already accepted that it is true and that the reckoning is real. The passage thereby establishes that concealment often runs on belief rather than on doubt, which is a harder position than plain denial.

crossReferences.why: Records the same doubled speech earlier in this surah, with the same verb for private company.
Describes a scripture put on sheets with parts displayed and much of it kept from view.
Says people hide from others what they cannot hide from God, who is present as they plan.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true that you know and have not passed on because it would be inconvenient for you if the other person had it. A piece of feedback, a fact about a shared decision. You do not have to hand it over today. Just notice that your reason for holding it is that it is true.

studies.title: Knowing The Book By Hearsay
studies.meaning: Two ayat describing two different problems. The first is a question put to those who calculate what to say in public and what in private, and it simply names the scope of what is known. The second turns to a much larger group who cannot read the text at all and hold it only as things heard and hoped. The word for what they have is read by commentators either as wishful notions or as recitations carried without understanding, and both senses are recorded. The closing verb places them in conjecture rather than in denial.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the surah's account of the communities around the young Muslim city. Literacy in seventh-century Arabia was rare and specialised, so for most people any scripture existed only as somebody else's recitation of it. Classical commentators read the second ayah as describing that ordinary condition rather than as a reproach, and distinguish it sharply from the deliberate reshaping described a few ayat earlier.

keyTerms.note: Describing a relation to writing rather than a quality of mind. The Quran applies the same word to the Prophet and to the wider Arab population who had received no scripture of their own.
The plural of a word covering both a hope entertained and something read aloud. Commentators record both senses here, and the two readings describe different failures that often occur together.

The state between certainty and doubt. Arabic gives it its own verb, and the Quran repeatedly contrasts it with knowledge, treating supposition as a poor foundation rather than as a mild form of knowing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing was a specialist trade. A small number in Mecca could keep trade records, and the scripture communities of Medina had trained readers who handled texts professionally. For everyone else a book existed as a voice: what a learned man had recited, what an uncle had repeated from him, what everybody knew it said. The distance between a text and the general belief about its contents was not a fault. It was the normal condition.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for those without letters is applied elsewhere in the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself, and in another passage to the community he was sent among. The same term therefore describes both a limitation being noted and a circumstance treated as significant, which is why commentators are careful with its tone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat name two ways of being wrong about a text, and only one of them involves any fault. Calculating what to reveal is a choice; inheriting a book as rumour is a circumstance. Placing them side by side makes access to knowledge a matter of justice as well as of effort, since the second group's position was created by others. The passage also treats supposition as a real category, neither knowledge nor lying.

crossReferences.why: States the principle behind the closing word, that conjecture avails nothing at all against the truth.
Uses the same word for the unlettered, describing the community a messenger was raised among.
Applies the same term to the Prophet, describing him as the unlettered messenger foretold before.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you are confident a text says, scripture or otherwise, that you have never actually looked up. Everyone has several. Find the passage today and read it yourself. Most of the time it will say roughly what you thought, and the value is in the small number of times it does not.

studies.title: Written By Their Own Hands
studies.meaning: One act is described with unusual precision: composing a text, attributing it to God, and doing so in order to obtain a price. The word of ruin that opens the ayah is then repeated twice more, once for what was written and once for what was earned, so the deed and its proceeds are pronounced on separately. Commentators divide over whether that opening word names a place or is simply an expression of doom, and most take it as an expression while recording the other view.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the surah's account of the communities around the young Muslim city. Classical commentators read the ayah as directed at a particular practice among some who handled texts professionally, and they are careful about the scope, since the surrounding ayat repeatedly distinguish a group from a whole. No individual occasion is reported with confidence, and the commentaries generally decline to name anyone.

keyTerms.note: A cry of doom rather than a curse pronounced on someone. Commentators differ over whether it also names a particular place of punishment, and most treat it as an expression of ruin.
Grammatically unnecessary, since writing is done by hand in any case. The redundancy is emphatic, insisting on the human origin of something about to be attributed somewhere else entirely.
The ordinary verb for earning a living. Its use here makes the proceeds a separate matter from the act, which is why the ayah pronounces on the two of them one after the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing was a paid trade, not a general skill. A small number of men drew up contracts, recorded debts and composed letters for others, and they charged for it. Attribution also carried a price everywhere: a line of poetry ascribed to a famous name was worth more than the same line from an unknown, and everyone in that world understood how much an attached authority could add to a text's value.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying they wrote it with their own hands is grammatically superfluous, since nobody writes with anything else. Classical commentators noticed the redundancy and read it as the point of the ayah, an insistence on the ordinary human hand behind something that was then given a different origin when it came to be sold.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two wrongs that would usually be merged. Attributing something to God that did not come from Him is one, and profiting by the attribution is another, and each is named on its own. That establishes that the gain is not merely evidence of the motive but an object of judgement in its own right. The ayah also assumes what it does not argue, that texts can be checked and origins matter.

crossReferences.why: Returns later in this surah to concealing what was sent down and taking a small price for it.
Asks who is more unjust than one who invents a falsehood against God or claims revelation received.
Describes tongues twisting the Book so a hearer takes for scripture what is not from it.

studies.applyIt: Check one thing you are about to pass on today, a quotation, a statistic, a claim about what someone said. Take the thirty seconds to find where it actually came from. Attribution is the whole subject of this ayah, and the ordinary version of the problem is repeating something confidently without ever having looked.

studies.title: Only A Number Of Days
studies.meaning: A claim of limited exposure is quoted, and the reply is built as a fork with only two branches. Either a pledge was taken from God, in which case it will certainly be kept, or something is being said about God without knowledge. The first branch is conceded generously, with a parenthesis affirming that God does not break a pledge, and that concession is what leaves the second branch standing alone. Notice also the verb in the original claim: the Fire will not touch them, which is the lightest word available for contact.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's account of the assumptions held by communities around the young Muslim city. A nearly identical claim is quoted in another surah with a comment attached about self-deception. Classical commentators pass on differing reports of the number of days being claimed and note that the Quran itself does not specify it, which is why the reply addresses the basis of the claim rather than its arithmetic.

keyTerms.note: The lightest verb in Arabic for contact, used of a hand brushing something. The claim is minimising in its very grammar, describing not exposure to fire but the possibility of grazing it.
A word used in the Quran for small finite quantities, including the days of the fast. Its presence turns an open danger into a manageable item with a stated length.
A binding undertaking, of the kind sworn before witnesses. The question asks for one in exactly that sense, which makes it a challenge with a procedure behind it rather than a rhetorical flourish.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A claim to hold a guarantee could be tested in that society, and everyone knew how. Who gave it, in what words, before which witnesses, at what gathering. Agreements were public by necessity because nothing was written down, so a person asserting protection could be asked to produce the occasion. The question in this ayah is that ordinary social procedure applied to a claim about God.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply grants the stronger of its two possibilities before ruling it out. It says that if a pledge was taken then God will not break it, which concedes everything the claim would need, and only then offers the alternative. Commentators note the structure, since an argument that first strengthens the position it is answering is unusual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What the passage objects to is not optimism but a claim made without grounds. A pledge from God would settle the matter completely, and the reply says so. The fault located is speaking about God on the basis of nothing, which the Quran treats elsewhere as a category of its own, distinct from denial and from error. Confidence about the unseen is presented as requiring a source, exactly as any other claim would.

crossReferences.why: Quotes almost the same claim about numbered days and attributes it to something they invented themselves.
States the general rule, not to pursue what you have no knowledge of, since every faculty is questioned.
Meets a comparable claim later in this surah by asking simply for the proof behind it.

studies.applyIt: Take one comfortable assumption you hold about how things will turn out for you, and ask yourself where it came from. Not to dismantle it. Just to find whether it has a source or whether it arrived by itself and has been sitting there unexamined since. Most of us have at least one of each.

studies.title: Encircled By What You Earned
studies.meaning: Two outcomes stated as a matched pair, with identical closing words, so the parallel is unmistakable. The conditions attached to them are not parallel at all. One requires wrongdoing that has surrounded a person completely, using a verb of encirclement with no gap left in it, and commentators read that as describing a total condition rather than any single act. The other requires belief together with good action. The particle opening the passage exists in Arabic only to contradict a denial, so the whole statement arrives as a reversal.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering directly the claim quoted in the previous ayah about a strictly limited exposure. Classical commentators read these two ayat as the correction to that claim, replacing a period of time with a description of condition. The pairing also restates in general terms a principle the surah has already stated elsewhere, that outcome follows what a person believes and does rather than what community they belong to.

keyTerms.note: A particle that cannot answer a positive statement. It exists solely to overturn a negative one, so its presence tells a reader that something just denied is being reasserted.
The verb for a wall going all the way round, used earlier in this surah of God encompassing those who deny. Applied to a person's wrongdoing it leaves no direction open.
From a root meaning to miss a mark, as an arrow misses. The word describes error and offence together, which is why commentators discuss whether it names deliberate wrong or covers both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Encirclement was a military and a travelling fact, not a figure of speech. A camp surrounded on open ground, a party caught in a gorge with both ends held, a settlement ringed by a besieging force: in each case what mattered was that no direction of escape remained. The word the ayah uses for wrongdoing that closes around a person carried all of that immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The particle that opens this passage is one Arabic reserves for contradicting a negative statement. It cannot be used to agree with a positive one. English has no single word for it, so translations reach for phrases like on the contrary or indeed, and the grammatical signal that something is being reversed goes missing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The asymmetry between the two conditions carries the meaning. Entry into the second outcome is described by two ordinary things, belief and good action, while the first requires a person to be entirely surrounded by what he has earned. Commentators press on that difference. It establishes that the two are not mirror images, and that the threshold described for the harder outcome is a totality rather than a count of offences.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle earlier in this surah, tying outcome to belief and action rather than to community.
Rejects reliance on wishes and attaches the outcome to what a person actually does.
Reduces the whole matter to weight, an atom of good and an atom of evil each seen.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between having done something wrong and being surrounded by it. The ayah describes the second, and most self-accusation confuses the two. Take one thing you carry as though it defines you and describe it instead as a thing you did, in one sentence, with a date attached.

studies.title: Speak To People Beautifully
studies.meaning: A covenant is recalled as a list, and the order of the list is the interesting part. It begins with worship directed to God alone, then moves outward through decreasing closeness, parents first, then relatives, then orphans, then the destitute. Only after all of that does it name how to speak to people in general, with no qualification on who they are, and then two practices. Commentators observe that the widest instruction in the list is the one about ordinary speech.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, recalling the terms of an earlier covenant within the surah's long address. A closely parallel list appears in another surah addressed to the community receiving the Quran, with the same opening and nearly the same sequence of people named. Classical commentators set the two passages beside each other and treat the shared shape as significant, since the same obligations are being described across different scriptures.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning both good and beautiful. It names treatment that goes past what is owed, which is why grammarians note that the sentence leaves its verb unstated and lets the noun carry the weight.
From the root for stillness and settling. The word pictures a person whom need has brought to a stop, unable to move on their own situation, which is a description rather than a category.

Attached here to speech and directed at people with no restriction attached. Commentators note the absence of any qualifier, and read the instruction as covering everyone a person happens to speak to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every group named in this list was a real position in Arabian society with real exposure. An orphan lost his protector and often his inheritance, since property passed through whoever was strong enough to hold it. The destitute had no institution behind them at all. Older parents depended entirely on the household they had raised. Naming these four in order was naming the people whose safety rested on nothing but obligation.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction about speech uses the general Arabic word for people with nothing added to narrow it. Commentators from early on have noted the absence of any qualifier and read the instruction as covering everyone, inside the community and outside it, which makes it one of the broadest single instructions in this stretch of the surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing ordinary speech in the middle of a covenant, between the people one owes and the practices one performs, gives conversation the same standing as the rest of the list. That is a substantial claim about where a life is actually made. The passage also runs from the vertical to the horizontal without a break, so that worship directed to God alone and kindness to a destitute stranger appear as items in one undertaking rather than as two departments.

crossReferences.why: Gives a closely parallel list, adding neighbours near and far and the traveller to the same sequence.
Expands the clause about parents into its own passage, down to the tone of voice used.
Restates the substance later in this surah, defining righteousness by what is given rather than by direction faced.

studies.applyIt: Take the instruction about speech literally for one day and apply it to the person you are least careful with. Not a stranger, and not someone you are trying to impress. The one whose reaction costs you nothing. Notice how much of your tone with them was running on the fact that it costs nothing.

studies.title: You Agreed And You Witnessed
studies.meaning: Two undertakings, and the pronouns are what carry them. The Arabic does not say do not kill one another. It says do not shed your own blood, and do not drive yourselves out of your homes, so an offence against a member of the community is described in the grammar as an offence against the self. The closing clause then adds two separate things. They acknowledged the terms, and they were present as witnesses to the acknowledgement, which forecloses any later claim not to have understood.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, recalling a further term of the same covenant. The ayah is the setup for the one that follows, which describes what happened to these undertakings in practice. Classical commentators read the two together and note that the surah states the terms in full before describing the breach, so that a reader has the agreement in hand before the account of how it was handled.

keyTerms.note: The specific verb for spilling blood, not a general word for killing. It names the physical act and its visible result, which is how blood claims were actually described and pursued.
The word covers a house, its enclosure and by extension a whole territory. Losing one meant losing standing, water rights and protection together, so expulsion was never merely a change of address.
From a root meaning to settle or come to rest. An acknowledgement in Arabic is a claim brought to rest, which is why the same root gives the words for a fixed place and for contentment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was the heaviest sanction short of killing. A man driven from his dwelling lost the protection of his group, his access to a well, and any standing in a dispute. The audience for this surah included people who had experienced exactly that, since the emigrants in Medina had left Mecca under pressure and arrived dependent on hosts. Nobody in that city needed the second undertaking explained.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic uses the possessive throughout, so the terms read as your blood and yourselves rather than as one another. Commentators treat this as deliberate rather than idiomatic, and it makes a community a single body in the grammar of the sentence before anything is said about it in the argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A covenant with two clauses about violence, stated in the language of self-harm, defines a community as something more than an association of individuals. That has a consequence the passage draws out in what follows, since a body cannot be selectively injured. The closing detail about witnessing also establishes that the terms were public. Nothing here was inherited unknowingly or accepted by default, which is what makes the account that follows a breach rather than a misunderstanding.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same construction in the community receiving the Quran, saying do not kill yourselves.
States the principle at full width, one soul taken counting as though all humanity were taken.
Describes those driven from their homes and property, and what is owed to them by others.

studies.applyIt: Think about a group you belong to and one person in it you have quietly written off. Family, workplace, community. The grammar of this ayah treats damage to them as damage to you. Test that today by doing one ordinary thing for them that you would do for someone you liked.

studies.title: Part Of The Book Only
studies.meaning: The undertakings just recalled are set against what was done with them. People of one community fought on opposing sides, expelled some of their own, and backed others against them, and then, when the same people came into their hands as captives, paid to release them. That last act was itself an observance. It is exactly the arrangement the central question names: holding to part of a scripture while setting aside the part that costs, and doing the first sincerely.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentators connect this ayah to conditions in the city before Islam, when its two main Arab tribes were at war and the settled communities holding scripture were bound by treaty to one side or the other. They fought alongside their allies against people who shared their own scripture and lineage, and afterwards paid the ransoms their scripture required for captives. The reports on this setting are widely given.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for a back. To do this for someone is to lend them your back, standing behind them in a fight, which makes the word describe alliance in its most physical form.
From the verb meaning to bind. A captive in that world was defined by being tied and by having a price, and the two facts together are what makes the following clause possible.
Shame that others can see, not private regret. In a society where standing was the whole of a person's security, this named a real and measurable loss rather than a feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina before Islam ran on cross-cutting alliances. A group could be bound by treaty to one Arab tribe while sharing scripture and ancestry with a group bound to the other, and when the tribes fought, the allies fought. Everyone in the city had lived through the last war or grown up on accounts of it. The situation this ayah describes was recent memory for the people hearing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The question at the centre of this ayah, about believing in part of a book and rejecting part, has become one of the most quoted lines in the surah. The case it was asked about is worth noting, since the selectivity described is not doctrinal. The clause that was kept was the expensive one to perform, and the clause set aside was the one that would have prevented the fighting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses to let one observance offset the abandonment of another, and it does so without questioning the sincerity of the observance. Ransoming captives was a genuine act of obedience. Crediting it against the expelling is precisely what the passage declines to do, which establishes that a scripture is taken whole or misused, and that partial keeping can look from inside like devotion.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who accept some messengers and reject others, seeking to take a way in between.
Speaks of people who made the revelation into portions, taking it in separated parts.
Shows the opposite disposition, hosts preferring others over themselves despite their own need.

studies.applyIt: Identify the part of a commitment you keep easily and the part you have quietly dropped, in the same area of life. Prayer and temper. Generosity and honesty. Diet and sleep. Write both down on one line. The ayah's question works because the two are almost always visible together once you look for the pair.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: The Present Bought With The Future
studies.meaning: The commercial image the surah has been using returns, and here the goods and the price are named exactly: the present life obtained, the hereafter paid. Two consequences follow and they are not the same. The punishment will not be made lighter, and there will be no help, so two separate hopes are closed rather than one. Commentators note the first of these particularly, since a denial of easing is different from a denial of rescue and shuts a door that would otherwise remain ajar.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, summarising the conduct described in the preceding ayah. Classical commentators read it as the assessment rather than a new charge, and note that the surah has now used the vocabulary of buying and selling several times in different places, always for the same kind of exchange. The audience for these ayat lived in a city whose economy ran on precisely this vocabulary.

keyTerms.note: The verb takes what is paid after a small particle, so the present life is what was obtained and the hereafter is the price handed over. Reading the grammar closely reverses the intuitive order.
From the root for lightness of weight. The denial concerns reduction rather than removal, which is a smaller hope than rescue and is closed here separately from it.
The verb for coming to someone's assistance in a fight, and the root behind the Quran's word for victory. It names outside intervention, the last of the four supports denied earlier in this surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravan trade was built on deferred return. Investors laid out capital in the spring for a payment that arrived months later, and the entire skill of the business was valuing a distant gain against a present need. Anyone who could not wait sold his share early at a discount, and everyone knew what that cost. The exchange this ayah describes was a familiar and expensive mistake in ordinary commerce.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for buying runs through this surah as a recurring image, used for guidance traded away near the beginning, for revelation exchanged at a low price, and here for the whole of the next life. Commentators note the repetition, and the accumulation makes commerce the surah's steadiest metaphor for how a person disposes of what they have been given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing the choice as a purchase makes it a valuation rather than a mere wrong. Something was assessed, weighed against something else, and preferred, which means the failure is one of judgement operating normally on bad terms. The passage also assumes the hereafter is a possession a person actually holds and can spend, which is a stronger claim than saying it may be lost. What is described is not a forfeiture but a sale.

crossReferences.why: States the misjudgement in its simplest form, preferring the present life while the hereafter is better and lasting.
Describes selling God's covenant and one's own oaths for a small price, and what follows from it.
Asks whether the enjoyment of this life is anything but a little compared with what comes after.

studies.applyIt: Take one hour you spent yesterday and price it in what it displaced rather than in what it contained. Not to feel bad about it. The exercise is simply to practise valuing a distant thing against a near one deliberately, which is a skill and not an attitude, and the ayah assumes it can be learned.

studies.title: Messenger After Messenger
studies.meaning: A long provision is summarised in one sentence: scripture given to Moses, messengers sent one behind another after him, clear proofs given to Jesus son of Mary and support given with the Holy Spirit, which the great majority of commentators identify as Gabriel. Then the question that turns the sentence around. What determined the reception of each was not the evidence, which the ayah has just described as clear, but whether the message suited the hearer. The criterion named is appetite.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's long address to those who held earlier scripture. The ayah compresses a whole history of prophecy into a single line and then asks about the pattern in its reception. Classical commentators note that the Quran repeatedly presents the prophets as one continuous succession rather than as separate foundings, and read the verb used here for sending as making that succession explicit.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for the back of the neck. To send messengers this way is to send each at the heels of the last, so the succession is described as a relay rather than a series of new starts.
From the root meaning the space between two things. A proof of this kind separates a claim from what it might be confused with, which is why the word is used for evidence rather than for wonders.
The same verb means to fall. Arabic pictures desire as the direction a soul drops in when nothing holds it, which is why the noun from this root is used for unchecked inclination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Messages crossed Arabia by relay. A rider carried word to the next stage, handed it on, and the message continued while no single person made the whole journey. Pilgrimage routes and trade roads had stopping places arranged for exactly this. The word this ayah uses for sending messengers in succession comes from that world, where covering distance meant one traveller arriving on the heels of another.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic changes tense in the middle of the final clause. Calling messengers liars is put in the past, while the killing is put in the present form. Grammarians and commentators note the shift, generally reading the present form as making the act vivid before the reader rather than as a statement about when it happened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grants the strength of the evidence before naming the obstacle, which changes what kind of problem is being described. If proofs were clear and support was given, then refusal is not an intellectual position but a preference. That is why the ayah names what the soul inclines toward rather than what the mind concludes. It also establishes prophecy as continuous, so that rejecting a messenger is a repetition rather than a new event.

crossReferences.why: Describes messengers sent one after another, each denied in turn by the community he came to.
Recalls the support given to Jesus by the Holy Spirit, alongside the signs he was granted.
Names the person who has taken his own inclination as a god, the failure this ayah describes in general terms.

studies.applyIt: Notice one piece of advice you rejected recently and ask whether you evaluated it or simply did not want it. The two feel identical from inside. A useful test is whether you can state the case for it accurately. If you cannot, you did not assess it, and this ayah is describing the difference.

studies.title: Our Hearts Are Covered
studies.meaning: An excuse is quoted, phrased as a diagnosis, and the single Arabic word for it is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions. One reading makes the hearts wrapped in coverings, like a blade left in its sheath. The other makes them vessels already full, with no room for more. Both are preserved and both are used in the commentaries. The reply does not accept the excuse as a fact about their equipment, and its final phrase is measured rather than absolute: they believe little.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentators report that some in the city had, before the Quran came, spoken of an expected prophet and looked to his arrival as an advantage against those who had no scripture at all. The second of these ayat turns on that expectation, describing recognition followed by refusal. The reports on this are widely given, and the ayah's own wording asserts the recognition rather than inferring it.

keyTerms.note: One written form with two established readings. As coverings it pictures a sheathed blade; as containers it pictures something already filled. Each yields a different excuse, and the commentaries work with both.
From the verb for opening a door, in a form meaning to seek. The Quran uses it for asking a decisive outcome, so the word covers both praying for victory and requesting a judgement.
Recognition of something previously encountered, distinct from learning it for the first time. The verb makes a claim the ayah does not argue for, that what arrived was already familiar to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both images behind the disputed word were everyday objects. A sword in its sheath was useless while sheathed, and a man drew before he could use it. A waterskin already full could take nothing more, however good the water offered. Anyone hearing the excuse would have pictured one or the other immediately, and either picture makes the same claim: nothing can get in here.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply ends by saying they believe little rather than that they do not believe. Commentators discuss whether this means few of them believe or that what they hold amounts to little, and either way the assessment is quantitative. Even in a passage of this severity, the wording stops short of describing an empty hand.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An excuse framed as a condition is answered here as a choice, which sets a limit on how far a person may describe himself as unable. The passage does grant something, since the reply speaks of a consequence following on refusal rather than preceding it. What is refused is the order of events implied by the excuse. The state is presented as arrived at rather than as the equipment a person was issued.

crossReferences.why: Records a similar excuse, that hearts are within coverings and ears carry a heaviness.
States the sequence the other way round, sealing following on the breaking of a covenant.
Speaks of those given scripture recognising it as surely as they recognise their own children.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the moment you describe an inability that is closer to a decision. I am not a morning person. I am bad at apologies. Pick one such sentence you say about yourself and restate it as something you do rather than something you are. Then leave it there. Naming it accurately is the whole task.

studies.title: Resenting Another's Portion
studies.meaning: A motive is named, and it is not disbelief in the message. What is objected to is the recipient: that God should send down of His bounty upon whomever He chooses among His servants. Commentators gloss the word for this resentment as both envy and overreaching, since its root means to seek beyond one's share. The transaction is then described as a sale in which the goods and the seller are the same thing, and the closing phrase doubles a single word rather than escalating to a stronger one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the surah's most direct statement of a motive for refusal. Classical commentators connect it to objections raised about the messenger's origin rather than about the message, and note that the Quran records comparable objections elsewhere, including a complaint that revelation should have come to a man of standing in one of the two great towns. The reports frame it as a dispute about who, not about what.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to seek. It slides between wanting what is not yours and going past a limit, so the same word covers envy and transgression without the Arabic having to choose.

The root means what exceeds a measure, what is left over beyond the amount required. Bounty in Arabic is surplus, which is what makes resentment of it a strange complaint about something nobody was owed.
The verb for going back to a place carrying something with you. It pictures a journey home with a load rather than a sentence handed down, so the outcome is described as brought back.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Distribution was the permanent source of grievance in tribal life. When a chief assigned water rights, allotted a share of spoils or arranged a marriage alliance, whoever was passed over remembered it, and the poetry of the period is full of such complaints preserved in verse for generations. Resenting another party's portion was not an exotic vice in that world. It was the ordinary substance of politics.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for God's bounty comes from a root meaning what runs over a measure, the part beyond what was needed. The same root gives the ordinary words for a remainder and for something spare. Resentment of bounty is therefore, in the language itself, resentment of a surplus that was never anyone's entitlement to begin with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Separating objection to a message from objection to its recipient identifies a refusal that no amount of evidence addresses, since the evidence was never the issue. The passage also describes the exchange as selling oneself, which collapses the usual distance between what a person trades and what a person is. And it names God's giving as unconstrained by merit, which is precisely the feature being resented.

crossReferences.why: Asks directly whether they envy people for what God has given them from His bounty.
Records the objection that revelation should have come to a great man of one of the two towns.
States the principle plainly, that bounty is God's and He gives it to whom He wills.

studies.applyIt: Notice one person whose good news you found harder to be glad about than you expected. Say something specific and true to them about it today, in one sentence, out loud or in writing. Not a general congratulation. Something that shows you actually looked at what they were given.

studies.title: We Believe In Ours
studies.meaning: The position quoted is not that the new revelation is false. It is that it is not theirs, and the sentence says so directly: we believe in what was sent down to us. The ayah then adds two things the speakers have not disputed, that it is the truth and that it confirms what they already hold. The reply that follows does not argue about the new revelation at all. It tests the claim to hold the old one against a record of how those who brought it were treated.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's address to those who possessed earlier scripture. Classical commentators read the exchange as a general pattern rather than a single occasion, and note that the reply reaches back into a history the speakers themselves acknowledged, which is what makes it an argument from inside their position rather than a challenge from outside it.

keyTerms.note: One of a small set of Arabic words that carry opposite senses. The dictionaries list it as meaning both what is ahead and what is behind, so the phrase covers everything outside the speaker's own portion.
From a root meaning what is established and rightfully owed. Arabic uses one word for a true statement and for a valid claim, so truth in this language is something with a right attached.

From a root meaning to bring news, or from one meaning elevation, and the lexicographers preserve both derivations. Either way the word describes a function rather than a rank held independently of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a tribal society the first question about any claim was whose it was. Alliances, feuds and standing all ran through that question, and assessing something on its merits before establishing its owner was not how disputes worked. The quoted sentence applies exactly that ordinary reflex to a revelation. It does not deny the content. It declines to consider anything that came from elsewhere.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word used for what lies beyond means both in front and behind. It belongs to a small group of words that carry opposite meanings, which the classical lexicographers collected and studied as a category of their own. Translators must pick one direction, and the sentence's reach in the original covers both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply establishes a method rather than winning a point. A profession of loyalty to a source is measured against the treatment of what actually came from it, which is a test anyone can apply and which does not depend on agreeing about the disputed item. It also makes ownership irrelevant to truth. The passage grants that the revelation is not theirs in origin and denies that this has any bearing on whether it is true.

crossReferences.why: Answers a comparable claim by pointing to messengers who came with proofs and were denied anyway.
States earlier in this surah that the revelation confirms what its audience already possessed.
Describes the attempt to accept some messengers and reject others as taking a way in between.

studies.applyIt: Notice a claim you assessed today partly by its source: a news item, an argument, a piece of advice. Ask whether you could state it in your own words accurately. Where you cannot, you sorted it by owner rather than by content, which is exactly the move this ayah is examining.

studies.title: Clear Proofs, Then The Calf
studies.meaning: One short ayah completes the argument of the one before it. Clear proofs had been given, and what followed was not doubt or a slow drift but the making of a substitute while the messenger was briefly absent. The Arabic word for the wrong that closes the sentence comes from a root meaning to put a thing somewhere other than its place. Misdirected worship is therefore named not as an emotion or an opinion but as an object set down in the wrong location, which is what the whole episode literally was.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing a short sequence of arguments in the surah's long address. The calf episode has already been recalled earlier in this same surah and is told at length in other surahs. Classical commentators note that its brief reappearance here serves an argument rather than the narrative, supplying the counter-example to a claim about believing in what had already been received.

keyTerms.note: Evidence that separates a claim from what it might be mistaken for. The word carries no sense of overwhelming display, which matters here, since the passage is about proofs that were understood and then set aside.
A form of the verb meaning to adopt something as one's own. It implies deliberate acquisition rather than being given or misled into it, which is why the ayah needs no further explanation of motive.
From a root meaning to put something out of its proper place. The same root gives the word for darkness used earlier in this surah, since darkness is light absent from where it belongs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Arabia was personal rather than institutional. A chief's arrangements held while he was present and frequently unravelled when he was not, since there was no office to carry them in his absence and rivals moved quickly. An episode turning on what a people did while their leader was away for a matter of weeks was entirely legible to that audience, who had watched smaller versions of it repeatedly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for wrongdoing shares its root with the word for darkness that appeared in this surah's opening parables. Lexicographers explain both through the idea of something being out of its place, light absent from where it should be in the one case and an act or an object misdirected in the other. English keeps no trace of the connection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah names the shortest possible interval between evidence and its failure. Nothing here had faded with time or been passed down at second hand. The proofs were recent, witnessed and undisputed, and the substitution happened during a brief absence. Placed where it is, the example establishes that clear evidence is necessary and by itself insufficient, which is a claim the surah has now made about a sea, a revival and a mountain.

crossReferences.why: Describes the calf made from ornaments, a body that made a sound but could not speak or guide.
Records the moment itself, including the warning given while the messenger was still absent.
Recalls the same episode earlier in this surah, followed there by the pardon rather than by an argument.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you were shown clearly and now act as though you never saw. A test result, a piece of feedback, a pattern someone pointed out. Write the evidence down in one line, exactly as it was given to you. The gap between knowing and acting is the subject here, and writing it plainly narrows it slightly.

studies.title: We Hear And We Disobey
studies.meaning: The opening repeats an earlier ayah of this surah almost exactly, changing only the final instruction, which here is simply to listen. The answer quoted joins the two halves that ought to belong together and splits them: heard, and disobeyed. Then comes the strangest image in the passage. The calf is described as having been made to soak into their hearts, using a verb from drinking, which commentators explain by the way dye enters cloth and cannot afterwards be washed back out.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing this run of arguments in the surah's long address. Classical commentators note the near repetition of an earlier ayah and read the pair as deliberate, since the two versions of the covenant scene end differently and the difference is what each passage goes on to discuss. No separate occasion is reported for this ayah, which belongs to the argument rather than to an event.

keyTerms.note: In Arabic one verb covers hearing a sound and acting on what is heard. The quoted reply splits a word that does not normally divide, which is why the sentence is so jarring in the original.
A passive from the verb to drink. Commentators explain it by dye soaking into cloth: not something held in the heart but something taken up into its fibre, so it can no longer be separated out.
From a root connected to a staff or rod, and to breaking away from a group. Disobedience in the word is departure from a body rather than the breaking of a rule considered on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cloth was coloured by soaking. A garment went into the dye bath and the colour entered the fibre rather than sitting on the surface, which is why a dyed cloth stayed dyed through years of washing and wear. Anyone in that world had watched the process or worn the result. It is the exact image the commentators reach for, and the ayah reaches for it first.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah repeats an earlier one from this same surah word for word until its final instruction. There the covenant scene ends with remembering what is in the scripture; here it ends with listening. Commentators treat the pair as a single passage told twice with a different closing verb, and each version develops the verb it ends on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sentence quoted here has an exact counterpart elsewhere in the Quran, where believers answering their Lord say that they hear and they obey. The two replies differ by one word and the Quran preserves both, which makes the pairing a description of the only two things a person can do with something heard. The passage also treats devotion as absorbent rather than chosen, since what soaks into a heart was taken up before it was decided on.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answering form of the same sentence at the end of this surah, hearing joined to obeying.
Describes the response of believers called to judgement as hearing and obeying, in the same two words.
Quotes the same divided reply again, alongside the ambiguous word this surah later tells believers to drop.

studies.applyIt: Notice one instruction today that you heard clearly and set aside without deciding to. Not a rule you disagree with. Something you simply received and did not act on. Say the two halves out loud in sequence, what you heard and what you did. The sentence in this ayah works because it is so ordinary.

studies.title: Then Wish For Death
studies.meaning: A claim of exclusive entitlement to the next life is met with a test rather than an argument. If the final home is yours alone, then long for it, and the challenge is framed on the claimant's own terms. The second ayah reports that the longing never comes, and gives the reason as what their hands have sent ahead. That is the Quran's standard image for deeds: baggage dispatched forward to a destination, so that what waits there was already loaded and sent.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's long address to those who held earlier scripture. A closely parallel challenge appears in another surah, put in almost the same words to those claiming a special standing with God. Classical commentators note that the test is offered rather than imposed and that the passage reports the outcome as a prediction, which is what makes it a claim the Quran is willing to stake something on.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning free of any admixture. The Quran's word for sincerity comes from the same root, so a claim of exclusive possession is made with the language of something unmixed.
Related to the word used earlier in this surah for scripture held as mere wishes. It names desire directed at something not yet in hand, which is exactly what a claim about the next life is.
The verb for putting something forward or dispatching it in advance. Deeds in the Quran are repeatedly described this way, as goods sent on ahead of the traveller to a place he has not yet reached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travellers and traders sent things ahead. Baggage went forward to the next stage with an earlier party, goods were consigned to a destination before the owner set out, and a merchant arriving in a town found waiting exactly what he had dispatched and nothing else. The image behind this ayah is not a metaphor invented for it. It is how anyone moving across that country actually organised a journey.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for exclusive possession comes from the same three letters as the Quran's word for sincerity, which means being free of anything mixed in. Both describe something unadulterated. The claim being tested therefore uses, in Arabic, the vocabulary of purity, which is part of why the reply asks for a corresponding purity of preference.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test proposed treats desire as evidence. If a conviction about the next life were held as firmly as it is stated, a preference would follow from it, and the passage says the preference does not follow. That makes what a person actually wants a report on what a person actually believes, which is a harder standard than any form of words. The reason given also locates the reluctance precisely, in what has already been sent ahead.

crossReferences.why: Puts nearly the same challenge to those claiming to be God's friends to the exclusion of others.
Meets a related claim later in this surah by asking simply for the evidence behind it.
Describes people asking why fighting was ordained and pleading for a short delay, fearing what they claim to want.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you say you believe about what matters most, and ask what you would prefer if it were true. Not what you would say. What you would choose between two ordinary options this week. The gap between the two answers is small and specific, and it is more informative than any amount of restating the belief.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Thousand Years Would Not Help
studies.meaning: The observation is comparative and precise. Not eager for a good life, since the Arabic leaves the word for life indefinite, but eager for any life at all, on any terms. The wish attributed is a thousand years. Then the argument, and it turns on a rare verb meaning to shift something a little to one side. Being granted that span would not budge a person away from what follows, not because the span is short but because length and what comes after it are not measured on the same scale.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the challenge in the preceding ayat and functioning as its explanation. Classical commentators read the ayah as accounting for the reluctance just described rather than as a fresh charge, and note the careful comparison it draws, which sets one attachment against another rather than making an absolute statement about anyone.

keyTerms.note: The superlative of a word for avid, clutching desire. It describes wanting that has stopped weighing what it wants, which is why the object of it here is left as bare life without qualification.
From the root behind the word for a lifespan, which also gives the verbs for building up and inhabiting a place. A life in Arabic is something constructed and dwelt in rather than merely elapsed.
A rare doubled form meaning to budge something a small distance. The word makes the denial exact: not that long life is insufficient rescue, but that it does not move a person even slightly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long life was genuinely rare and genuinely admired. Infant mortality was high, fevers and raids took adults without notice, and a man who reached great age became a source of history for everyone younger, since he remembered droughts and battles nobody else had seen. Wishing for a very long life was not a strange wish in that world. It was the most reasonable thing a person could want.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere gives a figure close to the one wished for here, saying that Noah remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty. So the number in this ayah sits just beyond the longest span the Quran itself records for anyone, which suggests the wish is being stated at the outer edge of what could be imagined rather than chosen at random.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats attachment to life as evidence rather than as a fault, reading a preference as a report on what a person expects. Its argument is then about scale. Extension does not alter a relation, however far it goes, because the thing extended and the thing that follows are not commensurable. That is why the verb chosen is one of tiny movement, since even a nudge would imply the two were on a single line.

crossReferences.why: Gives the span of a thousand years less fifty for Noah's time among his people.
Describes the gathering as though they had lingered only an hour of a day.
Has people asked how long they remained on earth, and answering a day or part of one.

studies.applyIt: Work out roughly how many weeks you have been alive. It takes a minute with a calculator and the number is smaller than most people expect. Do not draw a conclusion from it. Just let the figure sit for a moment, since this ayah is arguing about scale and a real number is more useful here than a feeling.

studies.title: Brought Down Upon Your Heart
studies.meaning: An objection aimed at the carrier of the revelation is answered without any defence of the carrier. The ayah states what he did, adds that he did it by God's leave, and then lists three things about what was brought: it confirms what came before, it is guidance, and it is good news. None of those concerns the messenger. The place of delivery is also worth noticing. Not to the ear or the eye but upon the heart, which is where the Quran consistently locates the receiving of revelation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentators report that this ayah answers an objection raised about which angel had brought the revelation, with hostility directed at the bearer rather than at the message. The reports vary in detail and the commentaries generally give the substance without pressing the particulars, since the ayah's reply works by redirection rather than by settling any question about the angel himself.

keyTerms.note: Named directly, which the Quran does for only a few angels. Elsewhere the same figure is called the Trustworthy Spirit and the Holy Spirit, and commentators identify all three with one another.
Permission, from a root that also gives the word for an ear. Lexicographers connect the two through listening, so granting leave in Arabic carries the sense of having given something a hearing.

The place the revelation is said to have been brought down to. The Quran uses the same phrase elsewhere for the same event, so the heart rather than the ear is consistently named as the point of arrival.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The person carrying a message and the person who sent it were sharply distinguished in that world, and everyone understood the distinction. Envoys moved between clans under protection, and an envoy could be disliked without the message being answered. Refusing to deal with a message by objecting to its bearer was a recognised evasion, common enough that people could name it when they saw it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran says the revelation was brought down upon the heart, and uses the same phrasing in another surah describing the same descent. Commentators note that the heart is consistently named as the place of reception rather than the ear, which is why revelation is described throughout as something settled inside a person rather than handed over to him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply refuses to treat an angel as an independent party who could be an object of enmity in his own right. What is stated instead is agency: he brought it, by permission, from the one whose permission it was. That establishes something about how the Quran presents the unseen servants of God, who are never described as having interests of their own. The three descriptions that close the ayah then move the discussion back to the content.

crossReferences.why: Describes the Trustworthy Spirit bringing the revelation down upon the heart in clear Arabic speech.
Attributes the same descent to the Holy Spirit, sent down in truth to make the believers firm.
Describes the bearer as a noble messenger, possessed of power, obeyed and trustworthy.

studies.applyIt: Notice one message you have discounted this week because of who delivered it. A colleague you find tiresome, a family member you have stopped listening to. Separate the two once, deliberately: write down what was actually said, without the person attached, and read it back.

studies.title: Tossed Aside Every Time
studies.meaning: Three ayat, each narrowing something. The first gathers God, His angels, His messengers and then two named angels into one object of hostility, refusing to let opposition be directed at a part while sparing the rest. The second says the signs sent are clear, so refusal cannot be explained by obscurity. The third turns from incident to pattern, asking whether it is not the case that every time a covenant is made, some of them throw it away. Even there the wording limits: a group of them, not everyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the answer to an objection about which angel brought the revelation. Classical commentators read these three as the widening of that answer, moving from one angel to the whole chain and then to a record of undertakings made and discarded. The surah has by this point recalled several covenants, so the question at the end has a series of specific instances already behind it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to run past or overstep. An enemy in Arabic is one who goes beyond a boundary toward you, which makes hostility a movement rather than a state of feeling.
The verb for throwing away something judged worthless, casually and without looking. It appears again in the next ayah of the surah, where what is thrown is described as landing behind their backs.
A word of proportion rather than of totality. The surah uses such limiting terms repeatedly in this section, and commentators lean on them when explaining how far any of these statements reach.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Treaties between clans were public, spoken before witnesses and renewable, and a group that repudiated one did it openly because there was no other way to do it.
