studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Safa and Marwa are two rocky rises a few hundred paces apart at the edge of the Meccan valley, close enough to the House that a person could see both from the sanctuary. Before the sanctuary was cleared, statues stood on them, and the pilgrim traffic that passed between was part of Mecca's economy. The route was ordinary ground that thousands of feet had already worn smooth.
studies.didYouKnow: Safa and Marwa are named only in this ayah and nowhere else in the Quran. The verb for performing the Umrah also occurs here for the first time in the order of the text. The ayah closes with two names of God paired together, appreciative and knowing, a combination that appears again only at 4:147.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A place with a compromised past is reclaimed rather than abandoned. The ayah does not deny the history; it renames the ground by attaching it to God, which is a different move from pretending the idols were never there. The closing description of God as appreciative also reframes voluntary good: what is offered beyond requirement is received by someone who notices, and the receiving is described in the language of thanks.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for the marks of God and ties respect for them to what is in the hearts.
Describes the House itself as a place of return and safety, the sanctuary these two hills stand beside.
Recalls the family left in a barren valley near the House, the setting the classical accounts attach to these hills.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place you avoid because of something that happened there: a street, a room, a table. You are not obliged to reclaim it. But notice that this ayah handles a spoiled place by putting a better name on it rather than by staying away. Walk through one such place this week and see what happens.

studies.title: The Exception In The Next Breath
studies.meaning: A severe sentence is passed on those who hide what was revealed after it had already been made plain, and then, in the very next ayah, the door is opened. Three conditions are named: turning back, repairing, and stating openly what had been withheld. The third is specific to the offence, since concealment is undone by disclosure rather than by regret alone. The passage closes with two names of God rather than a verdict.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a long section addressing scholars of earlier scriptures in the city who, the surah says, recognised what had come and kept quiet about it. The commentators differ on how wide the address runs: some read it as directed at that specific group, others as a general statement covering anyone who withholds religious knowledge. Both readings are recorded in the classical works without one displacing the other.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of holding something back that others have a claim on, like a witness keeping silent in court. It does not mean lying; the offence is withholding what is true.
From a root meaning to mend what is broken, used of reconciling people and of repairing a wall. Repentance here is not only inward; it includes fixing the damage the concealment caused.
An intensive form of a verb meaning to turn. It is used of God and of the person alike, so the same word describes the one who turns back and the one who turns towards them repeatedly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Knowledge was property in seventh-century Arabia. A genealogist, a poet or a keeper of scripture held something scarce, and standing came from being the one others had to ask. Sharing it freely cost real position. Medina's learned men were consulted on lineage, contracts and disputes, and their authority rested on knowing what others did not. The ayah names an offence that would have felt to some like ordinary professional discretion.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for cursing appears three times in the first ayah of this pair, once with God as subject and twice for those who curse. It is one of the few places in the Quran where a human act of cursing is described as landing rather than merely being uttered. The exception that follows arrives in the next breath, before the sentence has time to settle.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pairing establishes that no sentence in the Quran is final while a person is alive. It also defines a specific kind of wrong: not disbelief, but the private management of what belongs to everyone. And the remedy is shaped like the offence. Where a general repentance would do for a general fault, here the passage asks that the thing hidden be brought out, which makes forgiveness partly a matter of repair.

crossReferences.why: Returns to concealment a few ayat later, there with the price taken for the silence made explicit.
Records a covenant to make the Book clear to people, and the throwing of it behind their backs.
Repeats the pattern of an exception granted immediately after a severe verdict, with its own conditions.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you have not said because saying it would cost you standing: an error you noticed, a credit that belongs to someone else, a fact a colleague needs. Say one of them this week, plainly and without a speech around it. The second ayah asks for exactly this, and asks for it before it asks for feeling.

studies.title: And Died In That State
studies.meaning: The condition attached is not rejection but rejection carried to the end of a life. Two verbs sit side by side, one for the state and one for the death, and the sentence turns on their meeting. What follows is not a description of punishment but of a verdict pronounced from three directions at once: God, the angels, and all people. The weight is in the unanimity rather than in the severity.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after a pair of ayat that opened a door for anyone who turns back. The placement is deliberate: having shown that repentance is available up to the last moment, the surah describes what happens when the moment passes unused. The commentators note that no specific occasion is reported for this ayah, and read it as the general counterpart to the exception just made.

keyTerms.note: The clause is what carries the whole condition. Without it the sentence would describe a present state; with it, the description only closes once the person can no longer change, which is the point being made.
The root means distancing and expulsion rather than the hurling of an insult. What is described is removal from mercy, which is why the same word is used of an animal driven away from the herd.
An emphatic word placed at the end to gather the three parties into one. It adds nothing new to the list; its work is to close it, leaving no quarter from which a different verdict could come.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Exclusion was the harshest sanction a tribal society had. A man cut off from his tribe lost protection, water rights and the blood claim that deterred anyone from killing him, and he could not survive alone in that country for long. Poets were paid to pronounce such expulsions publicly so that every neighbouring clan would hear. The vocabulary of this ayah borrows that world and moves it upward.
studies.didYouKnow: The three-part formula naming God, the angels and all people occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 3:87, and nowhere else. In both places the subject is the same: those who turn away after belief or after clarity. The two ayat are close enough in wording that the classical commentaries routinely treat them together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Judgement is tied to the end of a life rather than to any point within it, which is why the tradition treats no living person as beyond hope and no living person as guaranteed. The ayah also declines to describe a punishment. It names a relation instead, distance from mercy, and lets that stand as the harm. What is lost is nearness, and the loss is stated as a consensus.

crossReferences.why: Carries the identical three-part formula, there applied to those who turn away after having believed.
Draws the same line at the moment of death, closing repentance once the end is actually in sight.
Sets the widest possible opening against it, addressed to those who went furthest against themselves.

studies.applyIt: When you next find yourself deciding privately that someone has gone too far to come back, notice that this ayah puts that judgement after a death, not before it. You are not being asked to approve of anything. Only to leave the file open, since the ayah before this one was written for exactly the person you have closed it on.

studies.title: One God, Two Names Of Mercy
studies.meaning: The first ayah closes the previous sentence: the state described has no lightening and no reprieve. Then, with no transition, the subject changes entirely. A single God is declared, and the declaration is completed with two names both drawn from the root for mercy. The commentators note the abruptness. Nothing prepares the turn; the passage moves from an ending with no relief to the widest statement of relief in the surah.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the end of a passage about those who conceal and those who reject. The declaration of one God is not aimed at a named opponent; it lands in the middle of an argument as the ground everything else stands on. The classical sources record a report that a request to describe the Lord preceded it, and they read the long ayah of signs that follows as the extended answer.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to look or wait. The passive form describes being given time, the way a creditor waits for a debtor, so what is denied is an extension rather than a pardon.
An intensive form used of God alone. Its root also gives the word for the womb, so the vocabulary of mercy in Arabic is built on the image of what shelters and feeds something before it can ask.

From the same root but a form describing a settled quality that attaches to particular recipients. Pairing the two words is standard, and the tradition reads the second as narrowing what the first states without limit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's sanctuary held many gods, and each clan had one it favoured, which meant that religion and lineage were the same subject. To say there is one God was to say that the arrangement of alliances built around those shrines had no foundation. It also cut through the working assumption of the caravan world, where a traveller acknowledged whatever local power governed the road he happened to be on.
studies.didYouKnow: The declaration of oneness here runs to nine words in the Arabic, while the ayah that follows it runs to more than four times that, stacking sign after sign into one unbroken sentence. The classical commentaries treat the pair as a single movement: the claim stated as briefly as it can be, then the evidence laid out at length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Oneness is stated twice in one line, first positively and then by denial, and the two do different work. The positive form answers how many; the negative form removes the category of rivals altogether. Then the sentence does not end with power or majesty, which is what the surrounding context might lead a reader to expect. It ends with mercy, twice, and leaves that as the final word about who God is.

crossReferences.why: Follows the same structure, a denial of any other god completed by two names, there naming life and self-subsistence.
States oneness at the shortest possible length, and by denial rather than by attribute.
Gathers the names of God into a closing sequence, beginning with the same pair of mercy words.

studies.applyIt: Read the two ayat aloud, one after the other, and let the join be as abrupt as it is on the page. There is no bridge between them, and that is the point worth sitting with for a minute. Notice that a passage which had nowhere left to go turned, without warning, to mercy.

studies.title: Signs Stacked In One Sentence
studies.meaning: One sentence gathers the sky, the earth, the turning of night into day, ships on open water, rain, animals, winds and cloud, and calls all of it evidence. The list moves outward and then back: from the largest structures to the wind on a person's face. The closing phrase restricts the audience, not the evidence. What is required is not special access but the use of reason.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following immediately on the declaration that there is one God. The commentators read the two as a single argument, with this ayah supplying the grounds. The items chosen are not abstract. Every one of them belonged to the working knowledge of the audience: the sea route to Syria and Abyssinia, the rains that decided a year, the wind that either filled a sail or wrecked it.

keyTerms.note: The word means both difference and taking turns, from a root for succeeding one another. Night and day are being described as a relay rather than as two things that merely differ.
An intensive verbal noun for repeatedly redirecting something. Applied to winds, it points at their changing quarter, strength and season rather than at the fact that they blow at all.
Covers anything that walks or crawls on the earth, from an insect to a camel. The word is built on the verb for treading softly, so what it names is a thing noticed by its movement.
From a root meaning to tie or tether, as a camel is hobbled. Reason in this vocabulary is the faculty that binds a person to conclusions, and holds them there once reached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia's inland towns lived by two things arriving on time: the rain and the caravan. A late rain meant thin pasture, weak camels and a hard year for everyone; an early one filled the wadis within hours. Ships were known from the Red Sea trade, and every merchant had heard of a cargo lost to a wind that changed. This list is an inventory of the things that decided whether people ate.
studies.didYouKnow: This is a single sentence in Arabic with one subject and one predicate, held open by a chain of coordinated nouns. Several of its items reappear as separate signs elsewhere in the Quran, each given a whole ayah of its own. Here they are compressed, which the classical commentaries treat as deliberate: the argument is the accumulation rather than any one item.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The case for God is made from ordinary observation rather than from miracle. Nothing in the list is rare; a person who never saw anything unusual would still have all of it. That places the evidence within reach of everyone and shifts the question from what has been shown to what has been noticed. The final clause makes inattention, not ignorance, the thing that blocks the conclusion.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the opening pair of signs and adds what the reflection looks like: standing, sitting and lying down.
Takes several of these same signs and gives each one its own ayah, spread across a passage.
Lists an almost identical set of signs and closes each group with a different faculty being addressed.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once today and stand still for two minutes with nothing to look at in particular. Notice the direction of the wind and whether it has changed since morning. That single item is on this list, between the rain and the clouds. The ayah asks for attention before it asks for anything else, and attention is cheap.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: Rivals Set Up Beside God
studies.meaning: Some people set up rivals to God and give them the love owed to Him. The comparison that follows is not between love and hatred but between two intensities: believers are described as stronger in love. Idolatry is defined here as a misdirection of affection rather than a failure of reasoning. The second half moves to a scene later on, where power turns out to have been undivided all along.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the argument that follows the declaration of one God and the long list of signs. The target is not a doctrine held in the abstract but the attachment people had to shrines, patrons and inherited loyalties. The classical commentators point out that those addressed did not deny God; they placed others alongside Him, which is what the word for rivals is chosen to describe.

keyTerms.note: The singular is used of a thing set level with another, and in Arabic usage it often carries a note of competition. What is described is not a replacement for God but something placed beside Him.
The comparative is built on a root for firmness and intensity rather than for quantity. Believers are not said to love more often; they are said to love with a grip that holds under pressure.
The definite article makes it the whole of power, not a share of it. The sentence does not say God has more power than the rivals; it says power as such belongs to Him, leaving nothing for them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loyalty in Arabia was felt, not merely calculated. A man loved his tribe, recited poetry about its dead, and would fight for a patron who had once given him water. The idols at the sanctuary were bound into that web of affection, inherited from fathers and defended like family honour. Asking someone to give them up was closer to asking him to leave his kin than to correcting an opinion.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places in the Quran where love is used to define the difference between belief and its opposite. The sentence breaks off before its conclusion: the clause beginning with a wish that the wrongdoers could see is left grammatically unfinished, a construction Arabic uses when the thing seen is too much to state.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is presented as an affection with a direction rather than as a set of propositions. That makes the standard harder and more honest: a person can hold the right position and still have their love pointed elsewhere, and the ayah measures the second. The scene of recognition that follows implies that the misdirection is not permanent knowledge but a temporary mistake, corrected too late.

crossReferences.why: Lists the loves that can compete, family and wealth and trade and homes, and asks which is dearer.
Describes a love that runs both ways, God loving them and they loving Him.
Continues this scene directly, showing the rivals disowning those who loved them.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing you would find hardest to lose. Not the thing you should say, the actual one. Then sit with the fact that this ayah does not ask you to stop loving it. It asks whether something else is loved more firmly. Notice which answer came first, and be honest about the order.

studies.title: Every Rope Between Them Cut
studies.meaning: The scene continues from the ayah before. Those who were followed break away from those who followed them, and the bonds between them are described as severed rather than loosened. The word for those ties covers ropes, kinship and any means of reaching something, so what is cut is not only affection but access. The disowning comes from the leaders first, which reverses the direction of the original relationship.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, part of a passage arguing against attachments placed beside God. The commentators read those followed broadly: chiefs, ancestors, and the objects of devotion themselves, since more than one classical reading is recorded and none is decisive. The setting is a society organised by following, where a man's standing came from whose lead he took, which is why the picture of leaders walking away had force.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to make oneself clear of something, the same root used of recovering from illness. It is a formal severing, closer to a public disavowal than to a private change of heart.
Originally a rope used to draw water or to climb, and by extension any means of reaching a thing. Cutting them removes not just the bond but every route between the two parties.
An intensive form suggesting repeated or thorough cutting rather than a single break. Placed at the end of the ayah, it leaves the picture of something shredded rather than untied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A rope was one of the most valuable things a household owned. It drew water from wells that could run sixty feet deep, tied loads to a camel, and pitched a tent against wind. Ropes were repaired, not replaced, and a cut one was a small disaster. Using that word for human bonds put the loss in terms an audience felt in their hands rather than in the abstract.
studies.didYouKnow: The same verb for disowning appears twice more in the next ayah, spoken this time by the followers, so the root occurs three times across two consecutive ayat. Arabic uses that kind of repetition to show an exchange, and here the exchange is one-sided: the second disowning is only wished for, and arrives too late to be made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Authority borrowed from other people is shown to be temporary. Whatever protection a follower expected is described as evaporating precisely when it is needed, which makes the relationship look, in retrospect, like a loan taken against nothing. The passage does not say the leaders were lying at the time. It says the arrangement had no substance to deliver, and the discovery is scheduled for a moment when nothing can be done about it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the leaders a speech: they admit they had no power and only issued an invitation.
States that friendships turn to enmity on that day, with one exception made for the mindful.
Stages the same argument as dialogue, with followers and followed passing blame back and forth.

studies.applyIt: Think about one thing you do mainly because a group you belong to does it. Not a bad thing necessarily: a habit, an opinion, a way of spending an evening. Ask what would remain of it if the group were not there. You do not need to stop. Just find out whether it is yours.

studies.title: If Only We Could Go Back
studies.meaning: The followers answer with a wish rather than an argument: one more chance, and they would do the disowning themselves. The reply is not repentance. It is the same relationship reversed, which is why the ayah does not treat it as a change. Then the sentence turns, and their deeds are shown back to them as regrets, so that the works themselves become the grief rather than the punishment attached to them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the short scene that began two ayat earlier about rivals set up beside God. No specific occasion is reported for it. The commentators note that the passage is built as a scene of testimony in which each party speaks in turn, and they read the wish for a return as a recurring feature of such scenes across the Quran rather than a report of particular words.

keyTerms.note: A single instance from a verb meaning to wheel back, used of a horseman turning for a second charge. What is asked for is not more time but one more pass at the same ground.
The root means to strip bare or to exhaust, used of a camel worn out on a journey. The word names grief that comes from seeing clearly, when what was hidden is uncovered too late.

A causative form: the deeds are not simply remembered, they are made visible. The grammar puts God in the position of presenting the evidence, so the regret is produced by sight rather than by memory.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Raiding parties in Arabia turned and charged more than once in a single engagement, and a horseman who had missed his moment would look for another pass. The word used here for a second chance comes from that world. So does the picture of a camel driven past its limit, which is the image inside the word for the regret described in the second half.
studies.didYouKnow: The wish for a second chance recurs across the Quran and is never granted. At 6:28 it is answered directly: even if they were sent back, they would return to the very thing they were kept from. The word for regret here is in the plural, so what the deeds become is not one grief but many, counted separately.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Regret is described as a form of clear sight, not as a feeling added to a verdict. The deeds are shown, and the showing is the sorrow, which means the punishment described in this ayah is largely the truth becoming visible. That places a high value on seeing accurately now, while the sight can still change something. It also implies that nothing is added to what a person actually did.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same wish, saying they would return to what they were kept from if sent back.
Places the request at the moment of death, and closes the way behind the one asking.
Uses the same word for regret, spoken by a soul about the side of God it neglected.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you already know you will wish you had done differently: the phone call you keep not making, the apology you have drafted twice. This ayah is about the gap between knowing and acting closing at the wrong time. Close a small part of it today, while closing it still costs you only awkwardness.

studies.title: Footsteps You Follow Without Noticing
studies.meaning: The address is to all people, not only believers, and it opens the earth's food rather than restricting it. Two qualities are named together, lawful and wholesome, so the second is not a repetition of the first. Then a warning arrives that seems unrelated until the following ayah explains it. What is described is a sequence of small steps, and the third of them is speaking about God without knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a passage that turns from idols to the food customs built around them. The classical commentators connect it to pre-Islamic practices in which certain animals were set aside, released or declared untouchable by tribal decision, and note that those rules were treated as religion though nobody could say where they came from. The ayah addresses humanity generally rather than one community.

keyTerms.note: The root covers what is clean, pleasant and beneficial at once, and is used of good soil and of a pleasant scent. It adds a quality of goodness to what the first word settles as open.
The plural of a single stride. The image is of following a track step by step rather than making one decision, which is why the warning attaches to a path and not to an act.
From a root meaning to exceed all bounds. It names wrongs whose ugliness is obvious once seen, and Arabic uses the same root for a price that is outrageous and a wound that is grotesque.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food rules in pre-Islamic Arabia were local and unwritten. A clan might free a camel from work after a certain number of births, or reserve a particular animal for a shrine, and the reasons were remembered as custom rather than argued. Meat was scarce enough that these exclusions mattered: a household could go weeks without it. Rules that removed food from the table carried a real cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about following the footsteps of Satan appears in only four ayat of the Quran, twice in this surah and once each in surahs 6 and 24, and in each the subject is something ordinary: food, entering faith wholly, livestock, or gossip. The word for footsteps never occurs in the singular.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas are joined that a reader might keep apart. The first is that the earth's provision is open by default, so restriction needs a reason rather than openness needing one. The second is that inventing religious rules is placed in the same sentence as indecency, and given as the final step of the sequence. Speaking for God without knowledge is treated here as the most serious item on a short list.

crossReferences.why: Names the invention of food restrictions directly and calls the loss a self-inflicted one.
Warns against letting the tongue describe things as lawful or unlawful by invention.
Asks who forbade the good things God produced, and answers that they were made for people.

studies.applyIt: At your next meal, take one moment before eating to notice where the food actually came from: who grew it, who moved it, what it cost. This ayah puts eating and vigilance in the same breath. You are not being asked to eat less. Only to eat with your attention switched on rather than off.

studies.title: What We Found Our Fathers Doing
studies.meaning: The reply quoted here is not an argument but a preference: we follow what we found. The Quran does not answer it by defending its own claim. It asks a question instead, and the question concerns the ancestors rather than the practice, testing whether the people being imitated had understood anything. Inherited religion is not rejected as such; what is rejected is inheriting without ever checking the source.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the passage on invented food restrictions. The appeal to ancestors was the strongest argument available in Arabian society, where lineage carried authority and a practice's age was taken as evidence for it. The commentators note that the same reply is placed in the mouths of several earlier peoples across the Quran, which suggests it is being treated as a recurring human answer rather than a local one.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to happen upon something rather than to seek it out. The speakers describe themselves as having stumbled into their religion, which is a stronger admission than they intend to make.

Covers fathers, forefathers and the whole line behind a person. In a society organised by descent, the word carried legal and social weight, so appealing to it was closer to citing a constitution than to recalling a family habit.

From a root for showing the way, used of a guide leading travellers across country. The question pairs it with understanding, so guidance here is not a feeling of certainty but arriving somewhere real.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society kept its past alive by memory. Genealogists could recite a line of descent through twenty generations, and a man's rights to water, pasture and protection all ran through that line. Changing a practice his grandfather kept was not a private decision; it announced that the grandfather had been wrong, in front of everyone who shared him. The cost of the change was social before it was religious.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply about following ancestors recurs across the Quran in almost identical wording, given by different peoples in different centuries: at 5:104, 26:74, 31:21 and 43:23 among others. It is one of the most repeated pieces of direct speech in the text, and the counter-question is never answered by an appeal to a newer tradition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The counter-question sets a standard that applies in both directions. If a tradition can be checked against understanding and guidance, then so can a new claim, and the ayah invites exactly that scrutiny of itself. What is being refused is the move that puts a practice beyond examination by pointing at its age. That leaves reason with real work to do rather than reducing it to assent.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same reply in a food context and adds the clause about ancestors who knew nothing.
Traces the reply back through every warned town, and reports it as the standing answer of the comfortable.
Adds a sharper edge: they would follow even if Satan were calling them to the fire.

studies.applyIt: Choose one thing you do because it is simply how things are done where you come from. Ask a single question about it: what was the reason. If someone can tell you, you have gained a reason. If nobody can, you have learned something worth knowing. Either answer is better than the one this ayah quotes.

studies.title: Nothing But A Call And A Shout
studies.meaning: A comparison is drawn, and the commentators differ on how to read it. One reading places the rejecters in the position of the herdsman calling to animals that hear only noise; another places them in the position of the flock, hearing a call without content. The Arabic supports both, and the classical works record the ambiguity rather than settling it. Either way, sound arrives and meaning does not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the short passage that began with the appeal to ancestors. The three words at the end, deaf and dumb and blind, have already appeared earlier in this surah describing a different group, so the surah is reusing its own vocabulary. No specific occasion is reported. The image is drawn from herding, which was familiar to every listener regardless of their standing.

keyTerms.note: A specific verb for the cry a shepherd uses to drive sheep, not ordinary speech. It names sound designed to move animals rather than to be understood, which is what makes the comparison sting.
Two near-synonyms placed together, one for calling to someone and one for calling out loudly. Doubling them stresses that nothing arrives except volume, with no word inside it that could be answered.
Used of someone unable to speak from birth rather than someone silent by choice. Placed between deaf and blind, it completes a picture of channels closed rather than of a person refusing to use them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every family in Medina and Mecca knew sheep and goats. A shepherd moved a flock with a small vocabulary of calls, whistles and clicks that the animals learned as signals without ever attaching meaning to them. They moved because of the sound, not because of anything said. Choosing that scene put the whole argument inside an experience the audience had had before breakfast.
studies.didYouKnow: The three words deaf, dumb and blind appear together only twice in the whole Quran, at ayah 18 and here, both times in this surah, and with a different final clause each time. In the earlier place the clause says they will not return; here it says they do not use reason.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Rejection is presented as a failure of reception rather than of information. The message is fully delivered; what is missing is the faculty that turns sound into meaning. That protects the passage from becoming a complaint about stubbornness, and it also sets a limit on what argument can achieve. The Quran describes the condition without claiming that any human speaker can lift it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same three words earlier in this surah, closing with an inability to return rather than to reason.
Describes hearts, eyes and ears that exist but are not used, and compares their owners to cattle.
States plainly that the living and the dead are not alike, and that no one makes the buried hear.

studies.applyIt: Next time someone tells you something you have already decided about, try repeating it back in your own words before you reply. Not agreeing, just repeating. Most people find they cannot do it accurately on the first attempt, which is the small everyday version of what this ayah describes.

studies.title: Eat, And Then Say Thank You
studies.meaning: The address narrows from all people in the previous ayat to those who believe, and the instruction narrows with it. Where the earlier passage opened the earth's food to everyone, this one asks for something extra: thanks. The condition at the end is unusual. Gratitude is not offered as a reward or a courtesy but as the test of whether the worship claimed is actually directed where it is said to be.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the sequence about food that began by addressing humanity generally. The commentators note the shift of address and read the two ayat as a pair: the wider one settles that provision is open, the narrower one adds what believers do with it. The setting is a community whose food supply was uncertain enough that a full meal was not taken for granted.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word covering what is clean, pleasant and beneficial together. Here it stands alone without the earlier pairing, so the quality of the food is what the believers are pointed at.

The root is used of an animal that grows visibly fat on little pasture, and of a cloud that gives more rain than its size promised. Thanks in this vocabulary shows on the outside rather than staying inward.

A separate pronoun placed before its verb, which in Arabic throws the emphasis onto it. The word order does the work that English needs the word alone to do, and it is the hinge of the closing condition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina ate dates, barley bread and, on good days, a little meat or milk. A household's year turned on the date harvest, and a bad one meant real hunger before the next. Food arrived through hands you could name: the man who owned the palms, the neighbour who shared a slaughtered animal. Thanking God for a meal in that setting was not abstract, since the chain of giving was short and visible.
studies.didYouKnow: The conditional clause at the end reverses the expected order of words. In Arabic the object pronoun is placed before its verb, a construction the Quran uses in the opening surah as well, in the line about worshipping God alone. The same emphasis carries here, so the sentence asks whether the worship is exclusive rather than whether it happens.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is treated as the natural completion of eating rather than as an optional addition, and the conditional at the end gives it weight it does not usually carry. Taking a benefit without acknowledging its source is described, by implication, as pointing your worship somewhere else. That makes thanks a matter of accuracy about where things come from, not a matter of politeness towards God.

crossReferences.why: States the return on gratitude directly, and sets an increase against its opposite in one sentence.
Repeats the instruction almost word for word, there addressed after a passage about a ruined town.
Uses the same reversed word order to make worship exclusive, in the surah every reader knows by heart.

studies.applyIt: Say thank you out loud for one specific thing at your next meal. Not the meal in general, one item: the bread, the salt, the water that came out of a tap without your doing anything. Naming the particular thing is what stops gratitude from turning into a formula you can say while thinking about something else.

studies.title: The Clause For The Compelled
studies.meaning: Four items are named, and the restrictive particle at the front of the sentence limits the list to those four against the many exclusions people had invented. Then a clause is added for anyone driven to it by necessity, with two conditions attached that the commentators read as excluding appetite and excess. The ayah closes not with a warning but with two names of God about pardon.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering the food customs described a few ayat earlier. Arabia had a thicket of local exclusions, some tied to shrines and some to clan tradition, and no agreed way to settle them. The commentators note that this short list appears four times in the Quran, twice in Meccan surahs and twice in Medinan ones, with the wording nearly unchanged, which they read as a settled statement rather than a developing one.

keyTerms.note: A particle of restriction that fences a statement to what follows it. Placing it first turns the sentence from an addition to the existing customs into a replacement of them, which is the point of the ayah.

The verb is used of raising the voice, and of the shout that greeted the new moon. What it names is the naming aloud at the moment of slaughter, so the item excluded is defined by a spoken dedication.

A passive form from a root meaning harm and pressing need. The grammar removes the person's agency: they did not choose, they were pushed, which is why the clause reads as a description rather than a licence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Famine was a recurring fact in Arabia, not a rare disaster. A failed rain could empty a district, and travellers crossing empty country carried water and dates measured against the days ahead. People did die between wells. Every listener understood the situation the concession describes, because most families had a story about a year when someone ate what they would never otherwise have touched.
studies.didYouKnow: The same short list appears four times in the Quran, at 2:173, 5:3, 6:145 and 16:115, and in every one of the four the concession for necessity is attached in the same breath. The two Meccan versions and the two Medinan ones differ only in small phrases, which the classical commentaries take as evidence that nothing about it changed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The shape of the ayah matters as much as its content. A restriction is stated, and the exception travels with it rather than arriving later as a concession wrung out of the text. That builds a principle into the structure: hardship is anticipated at the moment the limit is given. And the closing names describe God as forgiving rather than as strict, which sets the tone in which the whole passage is meant to be heard.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same list in a Meccan surah, framed as an answer to what had been made unlawful.
Expands the list with detail and attaches the same concession for anyone driven by hunger.
States the principle behind the concession: ease is intended for you, and hardship is not.

studies.applyIt: Think about a rule you keep that nobody actually gave you: a standard for how a room should look, how quickly a message has to be answered, what counts as enough work. Write it down and ask where it came from. This ayah's whole force is in a single word meaning only, and shortening a list is sometimes the honest thing.

studies.title: Swallowing Fire Into The Belly
studies.meaning: Concealment returns, and this time the motive is named: a small price. What follows is not a threat about the future but a description of what is already happening, since what they take into their bellies is called fire in the present tense. Three consequences are then listed, and the middle one is the strangest: God will not speak to them. Silence is placed among the punishments.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, returning to a charge made fifteen ayat earlier and adding what was gained by it. The classical commentators describe learned men whose standing and income depended on questions being brought to them, and read the small price as covering fees, gifts and position rather than a single bribe. Whether the address is narrow or general is a point on which the commentaries differ.

keyTerms.note: The adjective is doing the work. No amount is named, so the price is small by comparison with what was traded away rather than small in itself, which allows the phrase to cover a fortune.
A deliberately physical word. The image moves the wrong from the tongue to the stomach, so that what was earned by silence is pictured as eaten, digested and carried around inside the body.
The same verb used earlier in this surah of what a messenger does for people. Its denial here is pointed: the very service they withheld from others is the one withheld from them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scholars and religious officials in Medina were supported by the communities that consulted them: gifts at festivals, a share of produce, standing in disputes over inheritance and land. None of it was secret or shameful. What the ayah describes is the pressure that came with it, when an honest answer would have cost the household its position and a careful silence cost nothing anyone could point to.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about exchanging revelation for a small price occurs several times in this surah alone, at ayat 41, 79 and here, and each time the subject is slightly different. The image of eating fire into the belly returns once more in the Quran, at 4:10, applied there to those who consume the property of orphans.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three consequences describe a relationship rather than a place. Not being spoken to, not being cleansed, and being left with pain are all losses of contact, and they answer the offence precisely: someone who withheld words is left without them. The ayah also treats income from a religious position as capable of corruption, which is a warning aimed at the devout rather than at their opponents.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of fire eaten into the belly, there for wealth taken from orphans.
States the same warning earlier in this surah, before the charge of concealment is made.
Repeats the denial of speech and of purification, there for people who sell an oath cheaply.

studies.applyIt: Look at one place where being honest would cost you money or standing. Not a dramatic one. The invoice you could round up, the review you could soften, the client question you could answer vaguely. Answer one of them straight this week and notice what the honesty actually cost. Usually it is less than the estimate.

studies.title: Deep Discord About The Book
studies.meaning: Two exchanges are named, guidance for error and forgiveness for punishment, and then the sentence breaks into an exclamation the translators handle differently: how enduring they are of the Fire, or what makes them so bold towards it. The commentators record both readings. The second ayah gives the cause. Disagreement about the Book is not a difference of opinion here but a split, and the word used describes standing on opposite sides.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage on concealing revelation. The second ayah widens the subject from a group to a principle: the Book was sent down with truth, and those who differ about it have gone far apart. The commentators connect this to the long history the surah has been recounting, in which each community received scripture and then divided over it rather than over anything else.

keyTerms.note: A commercial verb for purchasing, used throughout this surah for choices described as trades. It implies a deliberate transaction in which something was handed over, not a mistake or a drift.

From a root meaning to split something lengthwise, as a plank is split. Each party ends on its own side of the break, which is why the word suggests a separation rather than a quarrel that could be patched.
An exclamatory form built on the root for patience, which is why it puzzles readers. The commentators read it either as astonishment at their endurance or as a question about what emboldens them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade vocabulary sat at the centre of Meccan and Medinan life, and everyone knew the difference between a good bargain and a ruinous one. Caravans returned with ledgers of profit and loss recited aloud. Describing a religious choice as a purchase put it in the terms people used for their most careful thinking, where nobody accepted a bad exchange through inattention.
studies.didYouKnow: The exclamation in the first ayah is one of the few places in the Quran where the classical commentators openly disagree about the basic sense of a sentence rather than its application. The form can express wonder or ask a question, and the same consonants carry both. Major commentaries record the alternatives side by side without choosing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The second ayah locates the problem in people rather than in the text. The Book came down with truth, and the discord followed, which places responsibility for division on the readers rather than on any obscurity in what was read. That is a demanding claim, and it cuts in every direction. It leaves no group able to explain a split by saying the message was unclear.

crossReferences.why: Says the earlier communities differed only after knowledge came to them, out of rivalry between themselves.
Repeats the diagnosis: the division came after knowledge arrived, not before it.
Places the same account inside a longer history, where scripture was sent precisely to settle disputes.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement you are in where both sides claim the same source: the same rules, the same text, the same set of facts. Ask yourself honestly whether the source is unclear or whether something else is doing the work. This ayah says the second is usually true, and it says it about everyone, not only about the other side.

studies.title: Righteousness Is Not A Direction
studies.meaning: The ayah opens by denying that goodness consists in which way you face, then rebuilds it from the ground. Belief comes first, in God, the Last Day, angels, scripture and prophets. Then giving, described as money handed over while it is still dear to you, to six named kinds of people. Then prayer and regular charity, then keeping promises, then holding steady under persecution and hardship. The list ends by calling these people truthful, which is an unusual word to choose.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, shortly after the change of prayer direction had made orientation a public argument in the town. The commentators read the opening denial as answering that argument directly: people were disputing about east and west while the substance of righteousness lay elsewhere. Some classical reports connect it to a question put to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about what righteousness actually is, and the ayah answers by listing.

keyTerms.note: The root suggests wide open land, and the same word is used for dutiful kindness to parents. It carries generosity of scope, goodness that spreads outward rather than goodness that keeps rules.
A short phrase doing heavy work. The commentators read the pronoun as referring to the money, so the giving described costs something at the moment it happens rather than being surplus.

keyTerms.gloss: the traveller, son of the road
keyTerms.note: Literally the child of the path. It names someone cut off from their own resources by distance rather than by poverty, a category Arabian society understood as a specific and temporary vulnerability.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every group on the list had a visible place in that town. Orphans lost the protection of a father in a society organised entirely around male kin. The stranded traveller might be a merchant robbed on the road, wealthy at home and destitute at your door. Captives could be bought free for a price everyone knew. These were not categories of theory; they were people you passed between your house and the market.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the longest single ayat in the Quran, and its structure is unusual: it begins as a definition of an abstract noun and then switches grammar mid-sentence to describe people instead. Classical grammarians discussed the shift at length. The effect is that righteousness stops being a concept and becomes a portrait of somebody you could recognise walking past.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief and conduct are welded into one definition rather than listed as two departments of religion, and giving is placed before ritual in the order. Calling these people truthful rather than merely good suggests that the whole list is a matter of matching your words to your life. The passage also sets a standard high enough to prevent complacency and concrete enough to prevent vagueness, which is a difficult combination to hold.

crossReferences.why: Answers the question of who should receive giving with almost the same list of recipients.
Describes the steep path in similar terms: freeing a neck, feeding an orphan on a day of hunger.
Gives a parallel portrait of the successful, built from prayer, trust and keeping promises.

studies.applyIt: Read the list once and find the item you are quietly weakest at. For most people it is either giving while the money still feels needed, or keeping a promise nobody is checking. Take that one item and make it specific this week: a fixed amount, or a single commitment you honour on time. The ayah works as a mirror, not as a target to hit all at once.

studies.title: A Word Placed Where Pardon Begins
studies.meaning: A rule of equivalence is stated for a society that answered killing with escalating vengeance, and then the ayah spends most of its length on what happens if the injured family chooses not to take it. Forgiveness is given a procedure: a reasonable demand, paid in good will. The alternative is named as a lightening and a mercy, and the closing clause protects the arrangement from being reopened afterwards.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the first legislative section of the surah. Before this, a killing in Arabia set off a claim that a tribe pressed for as long as its honour required, and a strong clan could demand many lives for one. The commentators describe feuds that ran for generations over a single death. The ayah is addressed to a community that had lived inside that system and knew its arithmetic.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow a track exactly, step for step. The word does not mean revenge; it means measured correspondence, and the whole point of it is that the response cannot exceed the injury.

The one who caused the death is called the brother of the one seeking redress. Placing that word in the middle of such a passage is deliberate, and the commentators read it as holding open a relationship the crime would otherwise end.
The word describes reducing a weight rather than removing a claim. What is called light here is the alternative to retribution, which frames the whole arrangement as a burden being eased.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood claims were the closest thing Arabia had to a police force. Knowing that your tribe would answer for you was what kept a traveller safe, and knowing that the answer might be tenfold was what deterred an attack. The system worked and also destroyed families, since a feud outlived everyone who remembered its cause. Compensation in camels existed, but a proud clan could refuse it.
studies.didYouKnow: Roughly two thirds of this ayah is about the alternative to retribution rather than about retribution itself. The word used for the person who caused the death is brother, and it sits at the exact point where the family is considering pardon. The ayah that follows completes the thought with a line short enough to be memorised in a breath.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is defined as a ceiling rather than a floor. The equivalence exists to stop the response growing, which makes the rule a restraint on the injured party as much as a claim against the offender. Then pardon is placed above it and described as mercy from God rather than weakness in the family. The passage assumes that grief will want more than it is owed, and sets a limit on that.

crossReferences.why: Records the same principle in an earlier scripture and calls pardon an expiation for the one who forgoes.
Warns the one given redress not to exceed in the taking of it.
Sets an equal response beside forgiveness, and says the reward belongs to whoever pardons and mends.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who owes you something and notice how much of your attention the debt is taking. Not whether to forgive it, only how much room it occupies. This ayah spends most of its words on the road out, and calls that road a lightening. Ask what taking it would free up in your week.

studies.title: Life Inside The Rule Itself
studies.meaning: The first line makes a claim that sounds paradoxical: a rule about killing is described as containing life. The commentators explain that a known and limited response deters, and also stops the spiral that a limitless one produces. Then the passage turns to what a person leaves behind, asking that a testament be made for parents and near relatives, done fairly. The two subjects share a setting: what happens to a family after a death.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the start of the surah's legislative section. Inheritance in Arabia had followed custom, with property tending towards whoever could fight for it, and widows and elderly parents often left with nothing. The commentators note that this instruction about testaments came before the detailed shares given in a later surah, and they differ over how the two relate.

keyTerms.note: The word is indefinite in Arabic, so the sense is a kind of life rather than life itself. That softens the claim into something specific: the ordinary living a settled community can do once the feuds have stopped.
The second word means the kernel of a nut, the part inside the shell. Those addressed are described as having got to the core of a thing, which is a compliment paid before the argument is made.

Literally good, used here for property, which is how Arabic often names possessions. The choice of word treats what a person leaves as something good rather than neutral, and so as something with a claim on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A death in Medina reorganised a household immediately. Palm groves, a house, a few animals and any debts owed to the dead man all had to be sorted out by people who were also grieving, and old parents had no earning power to fall back on. Written wills were rare; most arrangements were spoken before witnesses and remembered. That is why the passage that follows worries about alteration.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening clause of the first ayah is four words long in Arabic, and it is one of the most quoted sentences in Arabic writing on law and rhetoric. Classical works on the Quran's style set it beside a pre-Islamic saying of similar sense, and use the comparison to make a point about compression.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Both halves treat the family as the unit that has to be protected, and both work by anticipating what people will do when they are least reasonable. Grief wants revenge; heirs want everything. The passage answers each by fixing something in advance, while the person is still calm enough to fix it. That is a particular view of human nature: not wicked, but unreliable at exactly the wrong moment.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the detailed shares of inheritance, which the commentators discuss in relation to this instruction.
Continues directly, addressing what happens when a testament is altered or drawn up unfairly.
Places parents at the centre of what is owed, in the language of lowering a wing to them.

studies.applyIt: Tell someone this week what you would want done if you were not there: where a password is kept, which cousin should be called, what you would not want fought over. It is an awkward conversation and it takes ten minutes. This passage puts that conversation in the same breath as protecting a family from a feud.

studies.title: Whoever Changes What He Heard
studies.meaning: Two situations are handled in turn. Someone who alters a testament after hearing it carries the guilt himself, and the person who made it is left clear. Then a second case: someone who suspects the testament itself was slanted or wrong, and who reconciles the parties instead. The first is charged, the second cleared, and the difference between altering and mending is where the whole passage rests.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the instruction about making a testament. In a society where such arrangements were spoken rather than written, the witnesses were the record, and a witness who changed his account could quietly redirect an estate. The second ayah addresses the opposite worry, that a dying person might favour one heir unfairly, and the commentators read the two together as covering both failure points.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for putting one thing in place of another. It is the same word used elsewhere for altering scripture, so the offence is framed as tampering with a record rather than as simple theft.

A rare word describing a tilt away from straightness, used of a person who inclines without meaning harm. It is paired here with a stronger word for deliberate wrong, so the ayah covers both the mistake and the intention.
Placed at the end of an ayah about words spoken and then altered, the name is doing specific work. The original wording is described as heard by someone whose record cannot be edited afterwards.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Almost everything in Medina depended on witnesses. Sales, marriages, debts and bequests were spoken in front of people who would be asked to recall them years later, and a reputation as a reliable witness was a form of capital. Memory was trained for this, and a man known to have shaded his testimony once was finished. The word for altering carries all that weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used in the second ayah for an unintended leaning occurs only here in the Quran, and a related form appears just once more, in a different surah. Its pairing with a common word for deliberate sin lets the sentence cover an honest tilt and a dishonest one in the same clause.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guilt is attached to the act rather than to the outcome, so a person who set something up correctly is not held responsible for what others did to it afterwards. That is a precise idea, and it protects the dead as well as the honest. The second ayah then makes room for intervention: someone who steps in to repair a bad arrangement is cleared, which places reconciliation above literal execution of a document.

crossReferences.why: The instruction being protected here, about making a testament for parents and near relatives.
Asks those settling an estate to imagine their own children left behind, and to speak rightly.
Makes reconciling two parties a concern of the wider community, using the same verb for mending.

studies.applyIt: If you are holding a message that belongs to someone else, something you were told to pass on or a decision you were asked to relay, pass it on this week in the words it was given to you. Not improved, not softened. The distance between what was said and what arrives is where this passage puts the whole problem.

studies.title: A Practice Older Than This Community
studies.meaning: Fasting is introduced to the believers as something prescribed, and the sentence immediately places it in a longer history: as it was for those before you. The purpose given is not endurance or discipline for its own sake but attaining awareness of God, and the grammar leaves it as a hope rather than a guarantee. Commentators note that the practice is presented as inherited rather than invented, which softens what would otherwise be a heavy new demand.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the second year after the migration according to the classical accounts, when the annual fast was established for the community. The ayat that follow immediately name the month, allow for illness and travel, and state that ease rather than hardship is intended. The commentators read the sequence as deliberate: the practice is given, then its history, then its purpose, then its exemptions.

keyTerms.note: The root means to hold back or come to a standstill, and Arabic uses it of a horse that stops and of wind that drops. Fasting is described as stillness rather than as deprivation.
The passive of the verb to write, used across the Quran for what has been decreed. The image is of something entered in a register, which is why the same verb covers both instruction and destiny.
From a root meaning to shield or guard against. It describes a protective alertness before God rather than fear of Him, and here it is named as the whole point of the exercise.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia already knew fasting. Meccans observed a fast on a particular day of the year, Jewish neighbours in Medina fasted on fixed days, and Christian monks along the trade routes were famous for going without. The audience did not need the practice explained, only regulated. A month-long daytime fast in a place where the summer heat was severe and water was carried by hand was, even so, an unmistakable escalation.
studies.didYouKnow: The month is named only once in the entire Quran, two ayat after this one, and that single mention is also the only place the Quran names any month at all. The classical commentators noted the singularity. The reason given there is not the fast itself but the revelation: the month is identified as the one in which the Quran was sent down.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the practice in continuity with earlier communities makes it a shared human discipline rather than a marker of difference, which fits the surah's wider argument about one line of revelation. Naming awareness of God as the purpose subordinates the physical act to an inward result, so the fast is a means and can be performed without achieving anything. And the closing hope, expressed as a possibility, keeps the outcome out of the faster's hands.

crossReferences.why: Names the month, gives the reason, and states that God intends ease rather than hardship.
Follows the fasting ayat with the promise of nearness, which the commentators read as connected.
Shows an earlier fast, Mary instructed to vow abstention from speech.

studies.applyIt: Whether or not you are fasting, try skipping one thing tomorrow that you take without thinking, and pay attention to the first twenty minutes after you notice its absence. That gap is where the mindfulness in this line is supposed to appear. You are not testing your willpower. You are finding out how much of your day runs on habits you never chose.

studies.title: A Counted Number Of Days
studies.meaning: The first phrase limits the whole thing: a counted number of days, not a season. Then two situations are named where the days are moved rather than removed, and a third where a different provision stands. Commentators differ over that third clause, some reading it as an earlier stage later settled, others as covering people who can only fast with real difficulty. The ayah ends by preferring the fast without commanding it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the second year after the migration, when fasting was set for the community. The commentators record a genuine difference over this ayah: some hold that it described an initial arrangement in which a person could choose between fasting and feeding someone in need, later settled by the ayah that follows. Others hold that it always applied to those for whom fasting is a real hardship.

keyTerms.note: A plural form used in Arabic for small numbers, so the word carries a hint of fewness alongside counting. Naming the days as countable is itself a kindness, since a limit is easier to carry than an open one.
The word is used of what redeems a captive, so it names a payment that stands in place of something rather than a penalty for failing. That framing matters: nothing is being fined.

A reflexive form suggesting obedience offered freely, from a root meaning to comply. The same verb appeared earlier in this surah about the two hills, both times marking what someone does beyond what was asked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel in Arabia was slow and physically hard. A journey to Syria took weeks, and a traveller rationed water against the next well rather than against thirst. Illness, without medicine to speak of, meant weeks of weakness. The two exemptions in this ayah name the two states in which the body has no reserve, and everyone listening had been in at least one of them.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about a number of other days appears twice within two ayat, here and in the ayah that follows, in identical wording, and nowhere else in the Quran. Repetition of a whole clause at that distance is unusual, and the commentaries treat it as a marker that the two ayat are one statement rather than two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The structure keeps returning to the same principle. Something is asked, and in the same sentence the cases where it cannot be done are named, with an alternative attached. Nobody is left to work out their own exemption or to feel they have failed. The closing preference, stated as better for you rather than as a command, also leaves the reader's judgement engaged rather than replaced.

crossReferences.why: Continues directly, naming the month and stating the principle of ease behind these concessions.
States the general rule these concessions rest on: no soul is charged beyond its capacity.
Uses the same verb for volunteering good, and closes with God described as appreciative.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk to yourself about a day when you could not do what you planned. This ayah names two situations and provides for both without a word of reproach. Try borrowing that tone once this week when something goes uncompleted. Move it rather than adding it to a list of failures.

studies.title: The Month The Quran Came Down
studies.meaning: The month is identified by what happened in it rather than by its place in the calendar. Three words describe the revelation: guidance, clear proofs, and a criterion that separates one thing from another. Then the practical clauses repeat, and a purpose is stated in several parts, ending in thankfulness. The famous sentence in the middle states a principle wider than fasting: ease is intended, hardship is not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the second year after the migration. Ramadan already existed as a month in the Arabian calendar, and its name is connected by the lexicographers to intense heat. The classical commentaries connect the descent of the Quran mentioned here with the beginning of revelation in that month, and record differing accounts of exactly what the descent refers to.

keyTerms.note: The only month named anywhere in the Quran. Lexicographers connect the name to scorching heat, from the season in which the pre-Islamic calendar first fixed it, before the lunar year began moving it through the year.
From a root meaning to split or distinguish. It names the revelation by its effect, something that divides truth from falsehood, and it becomes the title of a whole surah later in the Quran.

From a root associated with the left hand and with what comes without strain. Its opposite in the same sentence is built on a root for what is hard to handle, so the pair sets facility against friction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabian calendar was lunar and observed by eye. Someone had to see the new crescent and report it, which meant a month began on testimony rather than on calculation, and cloud could shift the start by a day. Naming a month by sighting made the community's shared time depend on people looking up together at the same hour, from different parts of the same town.
studies.didYouKnow: Ramadan is the only month named in the entire Quran. The sentence about ease and hardship in this ayah is quoted far outside its subject, in contexts that have nothing to do with fasting, and the classical commentaries already treated it as a general statement rather than one tied to the month.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The month is tied to a book rather than to an event in nature or a founding battle, which is unusual among religious calendars. What is being marked is a text arriving. The purpose clauses at the end order themselves: completing the count, then magnifying God, then thankfulness, so the practice is presented as leading somewhere rather than as an end in itself.

crossReferences.why: Names the night of the descent and describes what happens in it, without naming the month.
Calls it a blessed night in which every wise matter is distinguished, using the same root as criterion.
Repeats the principle of ease directly, saying no hardship has been placed on you in religion.

studies.applyIt: Take the sentence about ease and hardship out of its month for a moment and hold it against something you are making harder than it needs to be: a task you keep restarting, a standard you set for yourself alone. Ask what the easy version would look like. That question is not a concession; it is in the ayah.

studies.title: The Answer With No Intermediary
studies.meaning: A question is reported about God, and the reply is unusual in two ways. It drops the usual instruction to the Prophet to say something, and answers in the first person directly. And it does not describe God's location but His nearness, then His response, before asking anything of the questioner. Only after the assurance does the sentence turn to what people should do: answer Him, and trust Him. The order places the promise before the condition.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, set among the ayat on fasting, immediately after the month is named and before the passage resumes its instructions. Several classical reports describe a question put to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about whether God was near enough to be spoken to quietly or distant enough to require calling out. The reports differ in detail and the commentators record them without settling which is primary.

keyTerms.note: Used of physical closeness and of kinship, since the related word means a relative. Nearness here is stated without qualification, which the commentators contrast with the distance the questioners assumed.
The noun for one act of calling out, not a general practice. Its use makes the promise specific: an individual call answered, rather than an assurance that God listens in general.
The same verb used a clause earlier for God answering, now turned back on the caller. The repetition makes the relationship two-directional in a single sentence, with the same word on both sides.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access to power in that world ran through intermediaries. Approaching a chief meant a relative to introduce you, a client relationship, or a gift, and the pre-Islamic sanctuary was full of objects understood to carry a request closer to a god. Petition was a chain of favours. A statement that the call goes straight and the answer comes straight removed every link in that chain at once.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the very few ayat where God answers a question about Himself without the intervening instruction to the Prophet to say. Elsewhere in this surah questions are introduced with that formula repeatedly, and the classical commentators point out that the grammar drops it here precisely where the subject is nearness, so the form of the sentence performs its content.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes petition unmediated, which has consequences for how worship is understood: nothing is required between a person and God at the moment of asking. It also ties God's answer to the caller's responsiveness without making the second the price of the first, since the promise is stated first and unconditionally. And its placement among the fasting ayat suggests hunger is meant to produce asking rather than merely restraint.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the invitation, call on Me and I will respond, and warns against disdaining it.
States the same nearness physically: closer to a person than their jugular vein.
Asks who answers the desperate when they call, and leaves the question standing.

studies.applyIt: Ask God for one specific thing today, out loud and in your own language, rather than in a borrowed phrase. Name it plainly: the actual worry, with its details. Many people find this harder than reciting, which is itself worth noticing. The promise in this line is attached to calling, and calling means saying what you actually want.

studies.title: Until The Threads Can Be Told Apart
studies.meaning: A restriction the community had been keeping is lifted, and the reason given is that they had been straining against it in private. The passage does not scold. It names what happened, says the turning has already been accepted, and moves on. In the middle sits an image of husband and wife as garments for one another. The day's limits are then drawn by what the eye can see.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the second year after the migration. The classical sources report with reasonable agreement that in the first period of fasting the night was more restricted than it later became, and that some found the restriction beyond them. The ayah is reported as the response, and its opening is unusual in acknowledging the difficulty before removing it.

keyTerms.note: The everyday word for what is worn. Applied to two people about each other, it carries covering, warmth, closeness to the skin and the ordinariness of something put on daily without thought.
A reflexive form of the verb for betraying a trust, with the object being the people themselves. It describes a private inconsistency rather than a wrong done to anyone else.
An ordinary word for a thread of cotton. The image asks a person to look east and wait until two strands of colour can be told apart, which is a test anyone can perform without an instrument.

The word for the edge of a piece of land or the blade of a sword, so a line that is sharp rather than vague. The instruction that follows is about not approaching the line, not merely about not crossing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody in Medina owned a clock. The day was read off the sky: first light in the east, the sun's height at noon, the length of a shadow, the last colour going out of the west. Farmers and travellers knew these signs the way a modern person knows the time without looking. Defining dawn by two threads of colour used a measure everybody already carried.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the longest ayat in the surah, and it moves through four different subjects without a break. The mutual garment image occurs only here in the Quran. The phrase about the limits of God appears several times across the text, but the instruction not to come near them, rather than not to cross them, is distinctive to this place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are done at once that religious language usually keeps apart. A difficulty is admitted, and the admission is not turned into an accusation; the response is a turning and a pardon before anything else. Then the ordinary closeness of a marriage is given a warm image inside a passage about restraint, which refuses to treat the physical as merely tolerated. The ayah ends by explaining rather than commanding.

crossReferences.why: Describes marriage as tranquillity, affection and mercy placed between two people as a sign.
Uses the same phrase about the limits of God, there with a different instruction attached.
States the principle of ease that this concession puts into practice, a few ayat earlier.

studies.applyIt: Notice the moment today when the light changes and you can first tell colours apart, or the moment it goes. Stand still for it. This ayah measures a whole practice by something you can see with your own eyes, and most of us have stopped looking at the sky for anything except weather.

studies.title: You Do Not Know What Is Good
studies.meaning: A hard instruction is given and the dislike it will provoke is acknowledged in the same breath. Then the sentence widens into a general principle that reaches far past its occasion: you may hate what is good for you and love what harms you. The final clause explains why, and it is not a comfort about outcomes. It is a statement about the limits of human knowledge, which is left as the last word.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the period when the community in Medina faced organised hostility from Mecca and was being told to defend itself, having been forbidden to fight during the Meccan years. The commentators describe genuine reluctance among believers, some of it moral and some of it fear, and read the opening concession as taking that reluctance seriously rather than dismissing it. The ayat that follow address specific questions arising from the same conflict.
